Speech:
Another amendment eliminates the special benefit rate of 75 per cent of insurable earnings for claimants with dependants. That rate is paid to claimants in the extended benefit period, and to those earning less than one-third of the maximum weekly insurable earnings, in the initial benefit period. Now, under the amendment proposed, that benefit rate is being brought into line with the standard rate of 662/3 per cent. The 1971 act acknowledged that the longer people were on claim, the greater would be their non-deferrable expenses, particularly if they had dependants. However, since 1970 a number of much more appropriate measures have been taken to increase support for people with families.
Most notable of these, of course, is the family allowance, which has tripled since 1971. For example, a man with three children between the ages of one and six, who received $18 a month in family allowance support in 1971, may now expect $66.24. That allowance, too, has now been indexed to rise with the cost of living. That increase, combined with the indexing of income tax, eliminates the justification for a special benefit rate for claimants with dependants.
I feel very strongly, not in any way denying the income need relative to size of family, that the use of demo-grants-in this particular case, family allowances-is a much more appropriate way to recognize the legitimate additional need based on family size, rather than through the unemployment insurance plan under which benefits are-and, I strongly believe, should be-essentially
wage-related.
Another amendment reduces the age from its present level of 70 years to 65 years at which people will no longer be covered by the unemployment insurance plan. That reduces overlapping of the program with others which are more appropriate, and provides improved support to this age group. People of this age will no longer be required to contribute to the plan, nor will they be eligible to receive benefits. The special retirement benefit, however, will be made available to persons at the age of 65 under the current conditions, that is, if they have a major attachment to the labour force, whether or not they have stopped working.
Members of the House will note that the removal of the earnings test for those who apply for a retirement pension under the Canada Pension Plan, the indexing of old age security and taxation, and the enrichment of the guaranteed income supplement which have taken place since 1971, will all combine to provide support for persons aged 65 and over, again, in my opinion, through much more appropriate methods.
Increases in these programs have been substantial since the introduction of the act in 1971. For example, the maximum retirement pension available under the Canada Pension Plan increases from $65 to approximately $130 on July 1 of this year. Old age security increased from $80 in 1971 to about $126 in 1975. The guaranteed income supplement also increased from roughly $34 for a single person in 1971 to $88 this year. In addition, the personal income tax exemption was increased by $1,000 for persons aged 65 to 70 in 1972. Last year, that exemption was indexed to rise with increases in the cost of living. Another consideration relates to the fact that it is virtually impossible-indeed,

at times almost brutal-to apply those aspects of the act which relate to availability and active job search in an effective manner to persons in this age group. The fact is that most of them have, in effect, withdrawn from the active labour force.
I know that the argument is made on occasion that these persons, having contributed premiums most of their working lives, are entitled to draw benefits from the program at the end of their careers. However, this is a fallacious argument. Unemployment insurance is like term insurance. It was designed to protect against certain situations which result in a temporary interruption of earnings. The entitlement to this benefit is subject to that and certain other specific conditions in the act. Equity, the payment of premiums, no matter for how long, does not carry forward entitlement beyond the conditions stated in the plan.
The principle of the termination of the need to pay premiums, and entitlement to benefits at a certain age, has been established for years. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971 set that termination date for premiums and entitlement at 70 years of age. That corresponded formerly to the age of eligibility of old age security, pensions, and so on. In all these programs, this was gradually reduced to the age of 65 which is now the age at which nearly all senior citizens enjoy state income-support programs.
Another important amendment will allow an extension of the period during which insurable earnings may be counted for benefit entitlement beyond the present 52 weeks to a maximum of 104 weeks for specified groups of claimants who find themselves out of the active labour force for periods of time due to reasons beyond their control. These groups include persons who are incapable of work because of sickness, disability or quarantine, persons receiving workmen's compensation, those claimants on approved training courses, and those who were inmates of penal institutions, all of whom can find themselves unable to get work after the period of their involuntary withdrawal from the labour force and when they are ready and able to rejoin the labour force.
It had originally been thought that the shorter eligibility requirement introduced in 1971 would obviate the need for such an extension. But experience has shown us in these last four years that a number of insured persons still have a requirement for it, and in order to ensure that these groups of people have full access to unployment insurance, this amendment is being introduced. Another feature of this amendment provides for an extension of the benefit period to 104 weeks for persons receiving workmen's compensation and for inmates of penal institutions. [...truncated]

having been able to get to the appeal board, having been turned down before the appeal gets started, will they go to the umpire, particularly when the decision is always unanimous, as it is in Prince George? The chairman will not consider having the appeal referred to some other tribunal.

Since the bill was not a money bill and since there was a backlog of legislation in the House of Commons, Bill S-10 was introduced directly into the Senate and received intensive study before being passed.
The feed industry in Canada does approximately $llA billion worth of business annually, and is the sixteenth largest industry in Canada. It employs approximately 10,000 persons and produces about nine million tons of feed each year for use by livestock producers in this country.
The present Feeds Act provides for the regulation of livestock feeds as to composition, packaging, and labelling. The provisions of the act include requirements for registration of feeds prior to sale and other measures designed to prevent the marketing of feeds that are not known to be consistent with current nutritional and health standards for livestock. This form of regulation also prevents feeds from causing adulteration of meat products used for human consumption.
The last major revision of the act was made in 1960. As most hon. members realize, there have been many advances in animal nutrition since that time, as well as in manufacturing, distribution, and testing of feeds. There are many new products now used in feeds that are not included under the present definition of feed and hence are not subject to regulation. Bill S-10 extends the definition of feed to all those products and ingredients used or able to be used, in livestock feeding. However, the new definition of feed is not intended to bring veterinary drugs subject to the Food and Drugs Act, or products subject to the Pest Control Products Act, under its control.
The definition of livestock has also been expanded to include fish, because fish are now being raised by commercial farmers for human consumption.
There is increasing evidence that the public interest or that of the feed users cannot be adequately protected with respect to feed quality without regulation in some situations at the farmer or mixer level. Just as with meat quality, effective regulation must involve plant inspection and regulations applying to the manufacturing process itself. This is necessary to prevent harmful adulteration of meats, for example, which may not be easily detected in time in the finished product.
Feeds can be carriers of disease-causing organisms, such as salmonella, and act as a reservoir for reinfection of animals. Eradication of such infections cannot be accomplished by checking feed for sale only. It is important that manufacturing plants be inspected and clean-ups be done. The changes proposed in Bill S-10 will give authority to

inspect manufacturing plants and to require certain levels of sanitation.

I am happy that this opinion was expressed because it is important that all legislation be consistent with the provisions of the Bill of Rights. The purpose of the amendment is to ensure that this board is a representative board, that it will not be captive either to a particular point of view, whether industrial or anti-industrial, or to a bureaucracy that might be less sympathetic than it should be to some of the representations that will be made to the board.
We believe that the important principle of ensuring an adequate public hearing has two elements. First of all, all those individuals or groups who have something important to say should have the right to have it said. Secondly, the board should be given sufficient breadth and fairness that all reasonable points of view also receive a fair hearing. We think it is important to build this principle into the legislation.
We believe the best way to do that is to add the amendment in the name of my colleague, and this would have two effects. First, it would ensure that the board which deals with questions often of conflict between the industrial and non-industrial sectors of Canadian society reflects both sectors as a matter of statute. Secondly, we suggest that the chairman of the board be a person whose non-partisanship and independence are beyond question.
Since the Public Service of Canada, as an enforcing agency, is often regarded as something other than independent from time to time in circumstances of this kind, we think it important, in the interests of guaranteeing independence, that at all times the chairmen of boards of this kind come from outside the Public Service of Canada.
I would point out to the House that this is not a new procedure; it is a procedure accepted by the House by way of amendment moved by this party when dealing with the ocean dumping bill. Perhaps it has particular relevance to environmental questions where the government, because it plays a regulatory role, is not in a position to be regarded as as independent as it might be in other circumstances. It is an important practice to continue to bring into our law, a practice that is already in the law in the ocean dumping legislation. I hope it is one that the House will accept at this time.

In 1972 unemployment insurance made up 1.51 per cent of the gross national product. We read in the Vancouver Province of June 19, 1975, headlines indicating that Ottawa will not compel workers to take jobs. We read that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) told the Senate Committee examining federal manpower policy that the government will not force workers to accept jobs they do not want. In a riding such as mine this sort of thing makes people very uptight, especially when they know about UIC ski teams and when they see young people walking around the cities or on the beach having a good time in the sun. They know there is 20 per cent unemployment in the Okanagan Valley, and that the mines and the lumber mills in the area cannot get enough people to work. No wonder a statement such as this makes them uptight and they write to their member of parliament.

I think we must decide whether this should be a welfare scheme or an insurance scheme, Mr. Speaker. I submit it is really a welfare scheme. It has taught people not to work and, as a result, we are losing the work ethic in Canada.
I know that the unemployment insurance offices have people in the field trying to police the scheme, but in most cases it is the innocent who get caught. Some people have worked 20 or 30 years, have paid into the scheme, and for some reason find themselves unemployed. Then they have to fall back on unemployment insurance. These people are not experienced in beating the system and we know that those who are experienced in this sort of thing are hard to catch. The easy ones are caught and an example is made of them. Usually they are quite innocent people who do not know how to manipulate the system.
At the moment there is a post office strike and some unemployment insurance offices are open on Saturdays so that people can get their cheques. This seems to suggest that a lot of people are abusing the system. They might not even be in the area or could be out working-they could even have two or three different names on the list.
The strike has taught us that we should stop mailing these cheques. People should go to the office to pick up their payment. After all, they are unemployed and should have more time than anybody else. They should be available when the payment is ready.
Unemployment Insurance Act

BasePK: 2995729

Speech:
Order, please. Yesterday a question of privilege was raised by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whit-by (Mr. Broadbent) and a related question of privilege was raised by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). On the previous day a point of order was raised by the hon.
Privilege-Ruling
member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) during the period set aside for responding to questions on the order paper.
Having regard to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Leeds, as I indicated at the time I have some concern about it in view of the fact that the hon. member was basically complaining about the fact that, in response to a question he had placed on the order paper, the reply by the government suggested that reference should be made to a certain citation in Beauchesne's which would indicate that the question was clearly out of order. The point of order raised by the hon. member for Leeds can easily be set aside directly, in the sense that, since there is no obligation on the part of the government to answer questions, there can be no point of order by an hon. member who has received an answer which is unsatisfactory to him. However, the matter is not quite so simple.
The point of order raised by the hon. member for Leeds two days ago raises a very important question. Since there is no obligation on the ministry to answer questions which are placed on the order paper, it has been the attitude of the Chair and the administration here that the Chair should not unnecessarily interpose itself between the question on the order paper and the response or lack thereof, as the case may be. That is to say, it has not been looked upon by the Chair as its obligation to examine with great scrutiny or great care the procedural regularity of questions put on the order paper. This is not to say that the Chair does not intervene; there have been many occasions when the Chair has intervened and suggested to hon. members that a question is clearly out of order and ought not to be put forward. However, that is about the limit of the intervention.
If it is seen that answers may be made with reference to the procedural regularity of the question, and that this in turn will cause a grievance or a point of order on the part of the hon. member who has put the question on the order paper, it certainly is not the intention of the Chair to change the practice of intervening or establishing a more substantial presence between the questioner and the person to whom the question is put. Therefore, I say at this point that the point of order is set aside but I propose to ask the House leaders and perhaps the procedure committee whether it is time for some organization, whether it be composed of administrative officials of the House, members of the Chair staff and/or members of the House of Commons, to formulate the responsibility of scrutinizing and intervening in respect of questions which are put on the order paper, so that those which are not in order will not proceed and, therefore, the situation cannot arise again. Again I say it is not the intention of the Chair to take that step, but I propose to ask the House leaders and, perhaps, in turn the procedure committee whether that might be a desirable development.
The point of order, as I say, is officially set aside on the ground that, since there is no obligation to answer a question, no point of order lies if an improper or unsatisfactory answer is made. But I will ask for advice as to whether something should now be done to determine whether some scrutiny should be made of questions put on the order paper, from the procedural point of view.

November 6, 1975
Privilege-Ruling
I now turn to the questions of privilege raised by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and the hon. member for Nickel Belt concerning the proceedings of the Royal Commission on the Concentration of Corporate Power. These questions involve the availability of, and charge for, minutes of proceedings of that royal commission to hon. members of this House. Both hon. members have raised a very legitimate and important grievance about a source of irritation affecting them in their work as members of the House.
Parliamentary privilege, of course, has very narrow scope, but I am sure hon. members are unanimous that it ought to remain that way. In effect, I suppose everything that affects the disposition of a member in his attitude toward his work, or the facility with which he is able to carry out his duties, could be construed in the widest possible sense as influencing or affecting his ability to perform as a member. However, that has never been the interpretation. In fact, the interpretation has been narrowed to almost physical resistance which prevents a member actually carrying out his ability to speak in the House or his ability physically to fulfil his duties as a member. I am sure I am on safe ground in saying that we would be unwilling to extend the privileges of Parliament to include complaints about the proper attitude or service, particularly of bodies that lie outside the parliamentary scope and in the area of a royal commission.
I say, again, that both hon. members have brought to the attention of the House-I hope with some effect-the practice of a royal commission in making available its proceedings to members of the House. I hope the point has not gone unheeded, but I must say that under the strict technical interpretation and very tight definition of a question of privilege that has been respected by this House for so long, in neither case does a prima facie question of privilege lie.

The bill contains amendments concerning the effect on pension entitlements of pensioners from one plan who become members under a different pension plan in some other service of the Government of Canada. These amendments relate to the report made by the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates to this House on November 6, 1973, that the various restrictions and limitations on the receipt of pensions should be removed in these circumstances.
In the light of this motion and report, the government undertook to conduct a complete review of the principles which should govern the pension plans for which it is responsible. As a result of this study the government has concluded that one of the basic principles under these pension plans should be that a person appointed to a position under a different plan should not forgo his pension entitlement. Another principle which was confirmed by this study as still being appropriate was that provisions of pension plans may vary for groups within the federal service. As a result, amendments are being introduced in the various acts where a restriction exists to permit a pensioner who is re-employed to receive his or her pension unless he or she again becomes subject to the same pension plan under which that pension was paid.
Provisions are also included to permit the transfer of pension credits from one government plan to another in certain situations where such transfer provisions do not already exist.
Those are the principal amendments of broadest application to several of these acts. In addition, there are numerous amendments consequential upon new provisions in other legislation or designed to remove anomalies in the interest of greater consistency, deal with problem cases and a variety of matters which have arisen in the course of administering the various acts to which this bill applies.
The bill proposes the introduction of contributions to the Judges Act, a feature which is common to most of the pension plans covering the federal public service. As hon. members will have noted, members of the judiciary appointed before February 17, 1975, will be required by this bill to contribute lVi per cent of their salaries toward the cost of the improved level of judges' widows' benefits proposed under Bill C-47. Judges appointed after February 16 will contribute 6V2 per cent of their salaries toward the cost of their own and their survivors' pensions.
This rate is the contribution rate also proposed under Bill C-23 for the new superannuation plan for Lieutenant Governors and is the same rate as is paid by Senators under the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act. Similarly, another amendment to the parliamentary pension plan will increase the rate of contribution to 6V2 per cent of the Prime Minister's salary in respect of the Prime Minister's pension. At the same time the minimum age at which a former Prime Minister can draw his pension will be reduced from 70 to 65, which is now a more normal age for the commencement of retirement pensions than when the higher age was introduced in 1963.
The increase proposed in the level of the pensions of the widows of former Prime Ministers from one-third to one-half of a former Prime Minister's pension corresponds to the increase proposed under Bill C-47 in the level of pensions for the widows of judges.

State Pensions
and there are favourable things to say about this bill. I also spent some time speaking critically in the sense that I was pointing out things not in the bill which ought to be there. These related to improvements in the pensions of public servants and others who come under the aegis of the federal government. Even though in much of what I said last night I was speaking critically, the general feeling of the House was that the changes I was suggesting should be considered, if not immediately then certainly somewhere down the road. In other words, the 30 minutes of my speech last night was the pleasant part. I left for today a part which might not seem so pleasant, at least to some hon. members in this House.
I regret very much, especially at this time when restraint is being proclaimed, that there has been included in this bill a very generous increase in the provision of pensions of members of parliament, members of the Senate, cabinet ministers and others. Some might say to me that all this bill is doing is relating our pensions to the amount of our indemnity, and because our indemnity has been raised, therefore it is appropriate to raise the potential pensions which are payable to members of parliament. However, the fact is that in a potential way this bill is increasing the pensions of members of parliament by 33 V3 per cent. I use the word "potential" because one's pension has to be computed on the six-year average. But that is the general effect of the bill, to increase the pensions of members of parliament by 331/3 per cent.
I said a moment ago that one has to have in mind the six-year average, but it is also a fact that the pay provisions of members of parliament passed earlier this year include escalation of 7 per cent in January, and so on down through the years, so that the total amount of pension which is available to a member of parliament is on the move. It keeps going up. At the present time, the maximum pension a member of parliament can draw is $13,500. That requires 25 years service, of course. That maximum will go up, according to today's pay scale, to $18,000.
I am glad my hon. friend, the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), is here so that he can put in his objections, just as I did not agree and muttered my objections last evening when he pressed so hard for the right of members of parliament to draw their pensions and also to draw salaries in the public service at the same time. That is in this bill. I do not happen to agree with it, but one has to lose some battles as well as win some. I point out that a 33 'A per cent pension increase is overly generous. I point out, also, that under the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, for ten years' service one gets a pension of 35 per cent of the average of his six best years. In the public service, it takes 17 V2 years to get 35 per cent. I point out, likewise, that for 20 years' service in this House one earns a pension equal to 65 per cent of the average of his six best years. It would take 32'A years in the public service to reach that level of 65 per cent.
Finally, I note that in the House, with 25 years' service one reaches a pension equal to 75 per cent of the average of his six best years. Of course, that 75 per cent level is never reached in the public service; the maximum there is 70 per cent for 35 years.

BasePK: 2996457

Speech:
Order, please. Pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 26, the hon. member has given the Chair notice of his intention to seek consent of the House to set aside a special time to debate the motion that the House do now adjourn for the purpose of discussing a specific and urgent matter, namely, that of the effect of the postal strike.
Motions of this sort respecting work stoppages in the country, particularly work stoppages in the public service-especially work stoppages in the public service that have gone on as this one has, for some three weeks- always cause great difficulty for the Chair. There are one or two contradictions which I am sure all hon. members will understand, the first being that since it has been the expressed will of parliament to give to workers in the public service rights that are akin to collective bargaining rights in the private sector, and therefore to include the right to strike, an immediate contradiction is posed if as soon as that right is pursued parliament is asked to consider it as an emergency.
The fact that the right to strike exists presupposes that when a strike in the public service is going to take place it will cause inconvenience of major proportions. Since that is anticipated, it is very difficult to say immediately that the exercise of the right to strike constitutes an emergency within the terms of Standing Order 26.
On the other hand, there is the contradiction that if Standing Order 26 exists for any purpose at all in order to move the House into a special session, surely a three weeks' strike in the postal service must be something which ideally comes within the four corners of that Standing Order, otherwise the Standing Order would not make sense.
The Chair, of course, must wrestle with these two contradictions every time a motion such as this is put in this kind of situation. There can be no question that the effect on the public that is described with respect to the proposed motion is very clear. It is, in fact, always a matter of critical importance when disruption of a national service of the nature of the postal service takes place. On the other hand, the language of Standing Order 26 makes it clear that if there is another reasonable opportunity afforded to hon. members of the House to discuss the matter, then Standing Order 26 ought not to be resorted to.
The fact is that, in the first place, not only today, which is obvious, but almost every day since the postal strike began or since the conflict between the postal negotiations and the wage and price legislation which is before the House began, this subject has formed a substantial part of the question period every day. I recognize that that tends to argue for both sides of the question. On the one hand, it argues that since there is the opportunity to use the question period, which has been taken advantage of, an emergency debate is not necessary; while at the same time it says that since the subject occupies half the question period every day, it is obviously a matter of importance which tends to come within the four corners of Standing Order 26. The fact of the matter is that the longer I go on with this reasoning, the further I get from a conclusion: I realize that.

We have problems in the periodical press industry, but I do not think this legislation is going to solve them. I suppose the basic one is that our population is fairly small and that it is divided into two major language groups. Of our 22 million people, approximately 6 million read in French and the other 16 million do their reading in English. To compound the problem, the English part of the industry is centred in the city of Toronto.

When making a comparison with other countries we find that magazines in Canada receive a smaller percentage of the total advertising dollar than those of other industrial nations. In Canada, this is approximately 2.3 per cent of the revenue generated by advertising, in the United States it is 6.5 per cent, in the United Kingdom 8.5 per cent, in France 16.8 per cent, and in West Germany 27.9 per cent. I sincerely question whether the Canadian publishing industry has in the past been publishing the type of material Canadians want to read. In a free enterprise system such as we have, whether or not you are going to sell a product depends primarily on whether people are willing to buy it. They will only buy your product if they feel it is useful or will enhance their quality of life.
I believe Canadian magazines today are not struggling because of Time or Reader's Digest but because Canadians, individually, think those magazines are not worthy of their support to anywhere near the degree the magazines expect. Legislating Time and Reader's Digest out of existence does not guarantee that the revenue will go to other Canadian magazines. Quite likely, a lot of it will just dry up. A larger amount will go to other of the media, such as television, if the CRTC does not have a hand in that. If the CRTC is the watchdog of Canadian television, why does it not say to these terrible multinational corporations that the NDP spout about so often, that this is non-Canadian content and therefore should not be used for tax purposes? This can be carried to ridiculous extremes.

It should promote the sale of its product and build a reputation over the years. When a document is exempt from production, regardless of the validity of reasons given for its exemption, the government leaves itself open to charges that it is trying to hide something which may be politically embarrassing or damaging.
In most cases the only defence against these kinds of charges is the production of the papers and, conversely, the only means to substantiate the charges is the actual publication of the documents in question. As a result, without being able to see the information which has been requested, we are left in a sort of daisy-plucking situation in regard to the government's motives; are they based on the expected criteria for the exemption of the production of papers or documents required for the effective functioning of government, or are they using the criteria merely to avoid political embarrassment?
I believe this kind of situation in the long run undermines the trust on which our democratic and parliamentary system is based. There are many arguments for greater accessibility to information, not the least being simply that both members of parliament and the public require as much information as possible if they are to make a meaningful contribution to the decision-making process.

Some civilizations are created in response to a challenge, but others succumb when overcome by too strong a challenge, a challenge they are not strong enough to withstand.
Recently we said that multinational corporations are challenging us too strongly, and their challenge is more than our young country can stand. We reacted by passing legislative measures which will prevent our being challenged too strongly and smothered by superior or stronger forces. Madam Speaker, in July, 1974, the people of Canada had an opportunity to vote in a general election. The main issue which developed during the campaign, an issue on which the people really decided how to vote, was really the suggestion by the Convervative party that inflation in Canada was so serious that what was required to stop the inflationary spiral, so adversely affecting all Canadians, was a 90-day wage and price freeze, following which a Conservative government would work out an incomes policy.
At the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) opposed a wage and price freeze, saying it would not work. He said inflation was an international occurrence that could not be stopped or controlled by any one country. The people in Canada by the thousands deserted the Conservative party, and to some extent the NDP, and elected, particularly in Ontario, Liberal member after Liberal member. They voted this way on the basis of the Prime Minister's promise to oppose wage and price controls.
Some 15 months later the Prime Minister, elected on his promise not to impose wage and price controls, comes to the Canadian people and says we must have those controls. He may be right. The situation may have changed, but neither he nor his ministers have yet explained to the satisfaction of the Canadian people what that change has been. Those trained seals who sit behind the Prime Minister, many of whom were elected on the basis of his promise to oppose wage and price controls, expect us to keep quiet and fall in line as they have done. We were not elected as Liberals and we are not obligated to the Prime Minister. We intend to keep asking the same kind of questions we were asking last year.
We have attempted, here in the House and in committee, to find out from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) what the inflationary problem is. We know that in the last year the cost of living has risen by 10.5 per cent. We have asked the Minister of Finance what his experts have told him they expect inflation to be in the next year. We have asked why the government thinks the situation is so serious it has to bring in legislation the like of which we have never seen in Canada in over 100 years, except during wartime. We have asked the Minister of Finance what he expects the anti-inflation program will do, and what the rate of inflation will be after the implementation of this program.
The Minister of Finance has completely rejected all invitations to inform the people about the estimates his experts have made. I think he owes it to the people of Canada to tell them what the situation is. After all, he is

proposing controls on all Canadians the like of which we have never seen except during wartime, yet he is refusing to tell us what the situation is, or is expected to be.
Some of us with some contacts have made some inquiries. I have before me the estimates made by a very respected non-partisan and non-political institute, namely, the Institute of Quantitative Analysis of the University of Toronto. Let me place on the record the kind of estimate they made with the help of their computer. Their computer is similar to that used by the Department of Finance.
They estimate that the cost of living for the next year, without the anti-inflation program and the controls the government proposes, would have risen from the IOV2 per cent increase we had in the last year to 11.3 per cent in the coming year. Let us look at what they tell us the increase in the cost of living will be in the next year with the control program. According to the Institute of Quantitative Analysis the increase in the coming year will be 9.6 per cent.

I suggest there are a variety of ways in which the minister could deal with this distribution system. There are some immediate ones he can look at. One would be an investigation under the Combines Investigation Act to determine whether there is some measure of monopolistic practice that is preventing adequate access to Canadian publications. The second thing might be to throw open some of the government's own retailing operations, such as Info-Can, across the country. Madam Speaker, this evening I wish to speak on a particular topic which comes within the scope of Bill C-71. Other members have spoken about other topics; with your approval I shall speak on something of great concern to sociologists and lawyers. Probably this is one of the most delicate and controversial subjects involving our criminal jurisprudence.
When we examine our rape laws, nearly every myth about women in modern society is encountered. What is particularly alarming is the great gap between society's changes in values and behaviour and similar changes in our laws. Before the early awakening of an enlightened society, a woman was considered a chattel or mere possession, and any violation of her was measured as a decrease in her value. In medieval law, rape was defined as "capturing or carrying away by force, and it may be applied to things as well as to women." Indeed, rape from the earliest times was looked on as offence against property. This type of attitude dies hard, if at all. Many believe that if a
woman is a sexual person, then she cannot be raped. Thus the woman is at fault, somehow "she provoked the attack." Such ideas are not easily disproven and are often absorbed by women themselves. A rape victim then begins to wonder whether if in fact she did not cause the attack.
Although these myths are rapidly disappearing, other equally outmoded ideas still surround the concept of rape. The most evident is the distinction between "good women" and "bad women." Often when an accused is charged with rape or a related offence, counsel cross-examines the complainant-to the point which some people regard as harassment-on her past conduct and general character. This type of questioning has been allowed as relevant to the issue of consent, and often it is used to attack credibility. Some contend it leads to the appearance that the victim is on trial.
The character of the accused, on the other hand, has not regularly been in issue, unless he puts it in issue. The prosecution is not permitted to question an accused about his character, unless be becomes a witness in his own defence and tries to present evidence of his good character, or other witnesses testify as to his upright character. Neither is the prosecution allowed to question the accused about his previous criminal activities. Therefore it has been quite possible that the previous convictions of the accused for rape would never be divulged in the course of his trial. This is in contrast to the severe cross-examination of the complainant as to her previous moral conduct.
In other criminal trials cross-examination such as this is not permitted. Under the new amendments, evidence of the victim's sexual conduct with a person other than the accused will be permitted only if reasonable notice in writing is given to the prosecution. The judge will then decide, in a hearing held in the absence of the jury, whether such evidence is necessary for a just determination of the case. The judge may permit cross-examination if these matters are particularly relevant. But it would appear that if this amendment becomes law, cases where such crossexamination is allowed will be very rare indeed.
Under the present code section 142 requires the trial judge to warn the jury of the danger of convicting the accused if the complainant's testimony is not corroborated. Under the new amendments the direction is abolished for all offences listed in that section, including rape, attempted rape, intercourse with a girl under 14, and indecent assault. This deletion of the warning is not to mean that a more lax standard of proof is to be applied than in other criminal offences; it simply applies the same standard of proof, that is, proof beyond a reasonable doubt. These amendments seem simply to place women on the same footing as men, and place rape in the same category as any other serious criminal charge, which is a step in the right direction.
Amendments to section 442 provide that where the accused is charged with rape, attempted rape, indecent assault, etc., the judge must consider excluding the public when an application is made for such exclusion by the accused or the prosecution. If the order is denied, reasons must now be given. An additional amendment extends the protection to any proceedings rather than restricting it to the trial itself. Speech:
Madam Speaker, I go back to this very specific example. Police officers, on behalf of all, governments and society, will attempt to preserve not only the citizens' life but also their property. They have to make a choice, and that choice is made on our behalf, in the name of society and that of this country's authority, namely to do everything to protect themselves and protect the citizens' life.
If gangsters use weapons, police officers must also use them to defend society and property. This is where the whole tragedy occurs; we are talking about it today and the Law Reform Commission, does the same and we will talk about it again if the minister honours his promise to proceed with an in depth reform of the Criminal Code.
When our law enforcement authorities obtain equipment which is at least equivalent to that which is available to gangster chiefs, forces are matched; laws must be applied on the basis of our trust in our police forces.
Well, it is the opposite which happens now in our society, for policemen are doing their jobs, risking their lives arresting gangsters, and often losing their lives or their limbs in the process, as was recently the case in Victoria-ville, Drummondville, Moncton and several other communities. Later on, gangsters are put in jail where they live in comfortable cells, judgments in their case are quickly rendered and, not long after that, we hear that they are out again and that they have committed other crimes. Who decided that they should be released and why? Very often, some of them are even paroled by mistake. Such was the case recently in Montreal. They have to run after the prisoner. Madam Speaker, the morale of our law enforcement authorities has never been so low. Even if we adopted the most beautiful gold-lettered Criminal Code unanimously endorsed by this House, if in daily practice we were not able to give our enforcement authorities the necessary confidence and the assurance that they are backed up by the legislative authorities, we would have wasted our time. This is true whether we want to maintain law and order or administer this legislation.


Criminal Code
Somewhere in this bill, there is a provision on road-side screening devices. It is the same thing. This is enforced every day. That is what is meant by protection of society. Many people would like to go through red lights and stop at green lights. That is what I would like anyway. But the law is not made that way, Madam Speaker. We have to abide by it. There must be some order in society. We really must have the mind and the will to enforce it.
That is why I cannot believe in the seriousness and goodwill of the government when it agrees that the Minister should put his head on the block on the matter of capital punishment, when we already have a legislation which is not enforced or which the cabinet refuses to enforce.
Madam Speaker, that is why I am very sceptical about the mini-reform which Bill C-71 constitutes; finally, it is nothing but a very superficial rewrite.
I would describe it as window dressing. It will allow some policemen to say that the federal Parliament takes care of order in society, but it will change nothing in the rising crime index in Canada, the failure of the rehabilata-tion program in the last four or five years. Nor will it change anything in the speed with which justice is done today. We need but look at the number of people who wait for months and months before appearing in court; nor will it change anything in the type of scandal we read about in the newspapers, and which are brought to light thanks to the extraordinary work of the Quebec Police Commission probe into organized crime. Full pages of it are published; yet, we had a Criminal Code. I remember how, in 1968, we studied the omnibus bill which dealt with all manners of subjects.
I remember the then Minister of Justice saying how wonderful the bill was, that it was a new approach. It was fantastic, it would allow the tracking down of gangsters to come, thanks to the use of electronic wire-tapping devices. Well, this is more of the same. It demonstrates once again that our approach is erroneous, that we are not really sincere in the fight against crime, that we are not really efficient in the rehabilitation of criminals.
Madam Speaker, I would like to reserve my remarks on this subject. Since it bears on general points, I shall certainly follow this bill closely and, unlike the minister, I am not overly anxious to approve a bill which, ultimately has virtually no meaning. It would be important to tell the minister that his endeavour, his patience in listening to us are basically a waste of time since this bill changes absolutely nothing but words; it contains no in-depth change.

Speech:
In order not to detain members, may I quickly acknowledge very sincerely the kind remarks that many have made on my appointment as Minister of Justice. It is a somewhat awe inspiring position when one considers the predecessors from both sides that have occupied the office in Canada. I say awe inspiring, and somewhat intimidating, knowing the very eminent counsel that occupy places in this House and also those in the House who, while not lawyers, have a very deep and informed interest in matters relating to our criminal law. I truly appreciate the comments and can assure hon. members that I have always tried to conduct myself with an open mind with regard to suggestions on policy coming from all corners of the House, and I shall continue to do so.
We have had a very thoughtful discussion on this bill and other matters relating to the criminal law and the administration of criminal justice in Canada. I am not able to deal with many of the points raised in the five minutes left to me. All I can do is deal with the very useful points that have been made on such questions as rape, bail, drinking offences, conditional discharges, comments about gun control, and other things, when the bill is in committee, which presumably will be next week.
Because the debate did range a little-and I think that was useful-I want to put the bill in perspective and make it clear that this is one of the series of Criminal Code amendments that this House has now become used to. We are putting through the House, almost yearly, amendments to the Criminal Code of a substantial, procedural and evidentiary nature in an attempt, in a very complex society, to keep the Criminal Code up to date in substance and direction. Bill 71 is one of the series of Criminal Code amendment bills offered in an attempt to keep the law up to date.
Many members touched upon a point with which I agree completely-that simply amending the law from time to time or annually adjusting the Criminal Code is not solely
Criminal Code
the way to deal with the criminal law and criminal justice system. This is an important bill which makes important changes to the law substantially and procedurally but, as hon. members have pointed out, there are many other things that have to be done and need to be done.
I want to assure hon. members that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and I will be introducing a further series of amendments to the Criminal Code which are more comprehensive than Bill C-71 and will contain very important measures relating to law enforcement, prevention and detection of crime, changes in the parole system, release of prisoners and many other matters of importance. Some members pointed out that we have to go further than simply amending the law; we have to be concerned about the administration of justice. I agree with that.
At the attorneys general meeting held in Halifax on October 23 and 24, I suggested to the attorneys general and got their consent and approval to the appointment of a committee to examine things such as the prosecutorial responsibility of government. This committee is now at work determining which level of government should be prosecuting which crimes, with the objective of determining which is the most effective rationale and effective distribution of prosecutorial responsibility in this country. I just want to read this into the record:
That the committee be further instructed to report upon the feasibility of specific actions that might be taken, in the form of administrative and other arrangements, for the more efficient utilization of available court facilities and prosecutorial personnel by both provincial and federal authorities in areas of prosecutorial responsibility that are of concern to both authorities.
That is a beginning in the way of dealing with the question that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) raised about the delay in the administration of justice. The object of that committee's work and my work is to ensure that where there are criminals and criminal activity, the matter is investigated, put before a prosecutor, put before a magistrate or judge and dealt with as quickly as possible.
Across this country there are very long case loads. There are long delays between an investigation and a conviction. That is bad for the administration of the criminal law. It is demoralizing to the police officer who, often at considerable danger to himself, especially one working as an undercover agent on a narcotics offence, often at great expense to the taxpayer, and after a long and most thorough investigation, to have to wait six or nine months or maybe a year and a half before the case comes to trial and there is a conviction. That is bad for the morale of the police of this country. It is bad in terms of the criminal community. They think they can take advantage of this system of delays that are occurring in the administration of justice. They feel that because the law takes so long to work, they have a certain immunity. It is also bad from the point of view of the community which asks, I think legitimately, whether in fact the laws of this country are being enforced. Those are three things to which we should address ourselves.
Other members touched upon the Law Reform Commission and its work. I simply want to put it in the context of this bill. The Law Reform Commission has done, and is doing, an immense amount of work in the area of criminal law reform. Over the next three of four years we are going

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on motion No. 5 to Bill C-41 respecting the stabilization of western grains. I am going to support this motion, which adds the following provisions to the bill.
(i)	depreciation on farm machinery and equipment used for grain
November 28, 1975

production or used in the farm business in respect of grain production and transportation;
(j)	interest charges incurred in respect of the production or sale of grain; and
(k)	producer levies in respect of this act.
These are to be added to the cost of production for the purpose of the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I am sure almost every member of this House will agree that interest and depreciation can be one of the larger costs of production. If we were going through this type of exercise of stabilization in business and in industry they would be very much in favour of including interest charges and depreciation in their costs. Interest is, of course, a real cost. In my opinion it must be included in any cost of production, whether it be farm, business or industry.
I want to speak about interest for a short while, and farm loans, especially those made to young farmers. The government has taken a good step forward in increasing the amount of these loans so that young farmers can more easily get into the business of farming. This is what we need in Canada-more young farmers. It has been shown that the average age of farmers is high. Therefore, as I say, more young farmers are needed. When a farmer goes to the farm loan people to get a loan, I am sure one of the main things they look at is the interest cost; how much interest he is paying on the farm machinery which he needs to operate his business properly.
When we look at stabilization bills we find the government does not believe interest rates should be counted as part of the costs of production. We went through all this in connection whith the stabilization bill which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) presented to us. Hon. members may recall that the Federation of Agriculture along with other farm organizations, made strong representations to the minister pointing out that interest charges represented a real cost and one which should be taken into consideration.
Consider what is happening to farming in Canada. Farming has become highly mechanized. The Minister of Agriculture himself pointed but that as a result of mechanization, farmers produce more than any other workers in Canada. This was made possible because of moving from a highly labour-intensive industry to a highly mechanized industry. In order to do this, of course, farmers had to borrow money, thus incurring interest charges which have been running at increasingly high rates. It is true that machines are labour-saving, but they represent a serious investment for the farmer concerned, and if we turn our backs on costs of this type when we consider any kind of stabilization bill, we are acting incorrectly.
If we follow this argument through, we find that depreciation becomes a more important factor than ever because of the high initial cost of farm machinery. Possession of one machine creates the need for another to complement the one you already have; the farmer immediately finds himself dependent on a series of costly machines and his concern about their depreciation is increased accordingly. While we are on the subject of depreciation, allow me to quote what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goodale) said yesterday in
Grain Stabilization
response to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). Speaking on motion No. 5, he said:
There can be no doubt that if you were to ask a producer a very blunt and straightforward question about what he views as being one of his most important cost items he would probably reply that it was depreciation. It was not very long ago that western grain producers were literally living off their depreciation. It is an item which is first and foremost on their minds. When one looks at the particular provision in the context of the grains stabilization bill, one can see that the inclusion of depreciation is not one that will enhance the protection this bill offers western grain producers.
That is quite a statement. Ask any farmer whether he agrees with it. The only part I agree with is that farmers have sometimes had to live off the depreciation on their machinery. They did not want to do so because it is not a good position to be in. However, farmers in Canada were sometimes obliged to do it because they were not getting their cost of production, or enough money to live on, out of the market. It did not enhance their operation, because what they were doing was taking out the money they should have been using to replace their machinery.
What happens when farmers do not have the money to buy new machinery? They borrow more money for that purpose, thus increasing their debt and incurring further interest costs, which in turn means a higher cost of production. They are not using their depreciation allowance in the manner in which it is supposed to be used. The statement the parliamentary secretary made shows he knows very little, or nothing, about farming or about what farmers have to go through. The depreciation provisions are there to enable a farmer to replace his machines. They are a legitimate cost for which provision is made by the Department of National Revenue. far too often the staff of the vehicle or the plane will evade the responsibility and fail to be firm with some rather flagrant breaker of the rules.

December 3, 1975

those who qualify so that they may have a fair chance to buy a house. This legislation will not do a great deal with regard to increasing supply and it will not help people with low incomes.
We need public housing. In this respect we had a substantial drop to 19.2 per cent in the 1974 budget. Mr. Speaker, I will not take very much time on this matter. As we all know this is a non-controversial bill but I think I should commend the government for bringing in this legislation. The government, of course, should be criticized for the length of time it took in awakening to the problems that have been encountered as a result of the low rate of interest.
I think this bill serves three purposes. It attempts to solve the problem related to the low rate of interest. Second, I think it adds flexibility in that the governor in

council can either lower or raise the rate of return. I understand it does not move in terms of allowing the rate to be lower than that which was originally applicable. The third matter involves the discontinuance of sales because the government, in its wisdom believes that the sales of these annuities has served its purpose. The government believes that the annuities have been superseded by retirement plans in the private sector.
Dealing with the first point I am amazed that the rate of interest encompassed by the legislation is only 7 per cent when we are talking now of an inflationary rate of around 11 per cent. One can see that the purchasing power has been eroded by some 3 per cent or 4 per cent. I am not talking about indexing in this bill, but I am saying that the government should have appreciated the circumstances which exist in terms of hardship when we look at a 7 per cent rate in respect of this bill compared to the inflation rate of 11 per cent.
My second point concerns the discontinuance of sales. The act was first introduced in 1908. The House leader of the New Democratic Party says that the bill was born at the same time he was. I think that is a commendable situation. It shows how long that member has been in and around this House and that since birth he has been interested in pension schemes. He still is. In terms of reviewing his concern in this area may I say that the bill was brought in primarily to give people the idea that thrift is a necessity in our way of life and that they should put something away for their old age. If those principles are still applicable the government should accept that.
Perhaps these sales have to be discontinued because there has not been sufficient promotion and because the rate of return is simply disgraceful. I respectfully submit that the private sector has not in fact taken over the necessary pension schemes that workers should have in Canada. The latest statistics in this area, taken in 1970, indicate that almost 7 per cent of the people employed by private companies are not receiving coverage. Therefore I take a very dim view of the government indicating that we will now get rid of this annuity contract, which in effect is a pension scheme, because the private sector has taken it over in a satisfactory way.
These are the only comments I have. My colleague, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), will be our only speaker following me with respect to this matter. We appreciate the fact that the government has brought in this bill and we appreciate the thinking behind it, but at the same time we say the government should be chastised for taking so long to realize that such a step was required.
In its recent report the Canadian Council on Social Development criticized the attitude taken by the government in stating, that the private sector has taken over in this respect. It stated that the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec pension plan have been downgraded so that the private sector could carry on, and it has reached the conclusion that there has been a dismal failure in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a few comments to the House at this time on third reading of this bill to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. I wish to say at the outset that I do so on behalf of the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), who is unable to be here today. I mention that because of the very excellent background work the hon. member performed which helped all members of the Standing Committee on Agriculture when they were considering this bill. Because of his background as a veterinarian I think it is appropriate that I mention the work which he did on this particular bill.
We on this side, as I am sure do most members of the House, support the bill. The only critical comment I can make is that it took the government so long to bring it to this final stage. First reading took place on October 21, 1974, well over a year ago. It is perhaps appropriate to note that this is fairly typical of the low priority given to new agricultural legislation. Perhaps we fail to appreciate the

genuine importance and value of agriculture in Canada today.
The members of the standing committee certainly appreciated the work done by, and the co-operation received from the various branches of the Department of Agriculture. I mention in particular the Health of Animals Branch. This bill amends an act which is over 100 years old. By the very nature of the Contagious Diseases Act, the Health of Animals Branch must be very closely involved.
I speak with some knowledge of various cattlemen's associations across Canada. They too had the co-operation of the Health of Animals Branch with regard to the many representations they made to the department on this bill. I am sure the same applies to other branches of the Department of Agriculture.
I wish to refer to the concern of cattlemen with regard to the shipment of calves from western Canada to Ontario and points east of Montreal. After many years, this legislation will now make it legal to ship calves a little faster from western Canada by way of Winnipeg and Toronto to their final destinations, mostly in Ontario. For many years there has been an obstruction in getting calves shipped here quicker and, consequently, getting them here in a healthier condition.
At one time trainloads of cattle had to be stopped every 36 hours for a feed and rest period. Through mutual understanding, and I stress that as it involves the co-operation of the humane societies, it is now recognized that if calves can travel faster and without unnecessary stops, they can go for periods of 42 to 58 hours, and perhaps longer. The theory is that the quicker they get to their final destination, even when longer hauls are required, the better the health of the cattle will be. This legislation makes this possible. It takes the authority for those regulations out of the Department of Justice and gives it to the Department of Agriculture where it belongs.
This bill will update considerably the amount of compensation for animals that fall down on the brucellosis test. This is a very timely topic. We have heard a lot in this House and across the country about brucellosis over the past two or three years, particularly the past six months. Questions asked in the House clearly indicate there have been some problems with brucellosis.
It was reassuring to hear from the representatives of the Health of Animals Branch who appeared before the committee that progress is indeed being made. I believe more progress will be made, and possibly there will be a complete eradication of brucellosis. As this bill provides higher compensation to cattle producers, hopefully there will be better co-operation. After all, when the compensation is not very high there is a tendency not to advise the proper authorities that there may be brucellosis in the herd. Therefore this is a very forward step.
I hope this spirit of co-operation between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the various branches of his department will continue when the regulations are being drawn up. They will of course be very detailed and involved. I am sure that many agricultural commodity groups will want the opportunity to take part in a continuing discussion when the regulations are being drawn up.
December 12, 1975

With those few comments, Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise that we in the official opposition clearly support this bill.

The idea occurred to me last night when I heard the results coming in about the new alliance in British Columbia that perhaps the day had come when the Liberal and Conservative parties in the House should move to make the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) the Prime Minister, formalizing the alliance federally as well as in the province of British Columbia.

As the parliamentary secretary has said, this is a new endeavour which is going in a new direction. This step will make the Industrial Acceptance Corporation, with assets of $2.1 billion, as referred to by the parliamentary secretary, the new Continental Bank.
I do not see the need for any more privately owned banks in this country, and I hesitate to change the rules of banking until we have had a chance to study the changes during the decennial review of the Bank Act in 1977. For reasons of that kind I do not really think we should be in a

hurry to get this bill through the House. I realize this bill is going to raise a lot of questions and, therefore, I have no opposition to referring it to the standing committee. I look forward to discussing the bill in the committee with the parliamentary secretary and other members. Hopefully we can learn a lot from that study and make some decisions that will help us in reviewing the Bank Act in 1977.
As I said yesterday, or the day before in the House, I would like to take a whole new look at financial institutions in terms of making them publicly owned institutions. To me the banks and financial institutions have a tremendous say in what happens in this country. They have an awful lot of economic clout. They work in many cases hand in hand with multi-national corporations, and they have objectives and priorities that are based along the same lines as those of large corporations. They are profit and corporate motivated, and I think that is wrong.
I would like to see a big bank in this country owned by all the people of Canada, operated as a public utility or a publicly owned institution. That is the direction I think we should be going. Therefore I do not feel any need to co-operate in the formation of a new bank.
I do not want at this time to hold up the bill. I should like to see it get to the committee in order that we might have a chance to ask a lot of questions, and a chance to offer some amendments. In this way we might have a real chance to find out the purpose of the Industrial Acceptance Corporation in wanting to make this move. There are a lot of questions to which I want answers. I want to know who the primary stockholders are; who owns the corporation, and who sits on the board of directors. I want to know what positions they hold with other banks and other financial institutions. In addition, I want to know who they have in the Senate; are there any senators who sit on the board of directors of this company?
Once again I note that this is a bill which originates in the other place. I have said in the House before, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said on many occasions, I do not see the need for the existence of the other place, and to me it is a slight to see a bill originating in or introduced by the other place. That is not a democratic institution, but one that we think should not exist. It is a place I think has many conflicts of interest, particularly when it comes to a financial bill or a bank bill. Many of those people sitting in the other place are sitting or have sat on the boards of directors of many financial institutions or banks, dealing with bills concerning banking. To me that is a gross conflict of interest. I think this House should deal with all bills that come before us in a public sense, particularly those that deal with banks and financial institutions.
As I say, I do not want to hold the bill up. I am looking forward to dealing with it in the committee, if it goes to the committee, as I look forward to dealing with similar bills involving banking and financial institutions that come before this House in the years ahead.

I suggest that this could be worked out and that protection could be given to people at that age who are actually looking for work and are capable of taking it. I should like to say a few words about the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West to delete the whole of clause 1, which would affect the sponsors of LIP and LEAP projects. I agree that that clause should be deleted. I assume that this presumption is put in there to indicate that he is not a government employee, yet he is selfemployed. He dreams up the project and he administers it. As soon as the project is over, he can draw unemployment insurance benefits and start writing his application under the Opportunities for Youth Program or one of the other programs, and then perhaps qualify again. ry as perennial students. They will be perennial sponsors of projects which they initiate. This is like planning your own business but not being allowed to decide when it ends; that is up to the ones who administer the project.
I am inclined to agree on the necessity to eliminate the whole clause rather than just the part contained in paragraph (2)(a), because I believe that although there are abuses, in the case of LIP and LEAP projects there is no need to establish under the act another category which I consider to be a political category. People in that category can provide employment and receive money for the project, and when the project is completed they can draw unemployment insurance. In many cases the length of employment may last no longer than the life of the project.
I hope the minister will give some consideration to amending the provision on retirement at the age of 65. It may not be so important in rural areas and in some of the urban areas where it is not hard to find a job, but it is of major concern in my area and in some other parts of northern Ontario where many people 65 years of age and over should be given special consideration.
I suggest that if the minister, who is also responsible for Manpower, wishes to do something in this field, he might allay some of my fears and the fears of some of my colleagues, and certainly those of some people who are about to retire, by considering the provision of a period of training before retirement. The aim of such a training program would not be the time of employment but, rather, the time of retirement. We might then be in a much better position to recommend to persons over the age of 65 that they retire, with the knowledge that the benefits they receive will be sufficient to allow them to maintain a reasonable standard of living.
Other countries which face this problem make sure that the pension plans provide in the range of 50 per cent of the salaries or wages earned in the five or six best years of employment, but we in Canada, despite the claim to the contrary of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), certainly do not come close to meeting the needs of many of the people who retire in this country. I hope that hon. members on all sides who are concerned with Canadians who have to retire at the age of 65 will give favourable consideration to the amendment before us, so that these people will find it less difficult to retire if they are allowed to do so gradually rather than being dumped off, as the hon. member who preceded me indicated, knowing that this Christmas will be the deadline for them.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, when I called it six o'clock I was trying to bring home to the government as vividly as possible the error of its ways in respect of the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which deal primarily with fighting the high cost of unemployment insurance on the backs of the poor.
I attempted to indicate that the reason the bill stands as it does is that the government, back in 1971, had some compassionate feeling for those faced with the high cost of food, shelter, and clothing. At the time the government felt that if a person had a family or dependants that person should be recognized as such. Now, as I stated earlier, it seems that the government is taking from the poor in order to give to those who are pregnant.
The government's reasoning now seems to be that it does not want the scheme to be a welfare scheme and is trying to move in the direction of a pure unemployment insurance plan or an insurance scheme. Let me point out that so far as this principle of unemployment insurance is concerned, it is destroyed once the government moves in the direction of recognizing pregnancy as a sickness for the purpose of the plan. It is interesting to note that the government did not move in this regard in violation of the principle, but rather in favour of pregnancy, making coverage even more flexible. It seems to me there is an undue amount of hardship being placed on those who are at the bottom of the economic ladder, at this particular time of high inflation and high cost of living, making these people feel the pinch even more.
What is even more strange is that the clause, as I understand it, subject to check by the minister in his usual style, is talking about $5 per person. This is the type of saving the government anticipates when it is referring to savings of some $30 million.
I was impressed by one or two briefs that were presented to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration when it dealt with the bill clause by clause. We heard from the Council on Social Development, represented by Mr. Reuben Baetz, and we also heard from the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I express my appreciation to those people for having taken part in what I felt at the time, and now know, was a very significant debate.
Let me read just one part of the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress. I realize I may be repetitious in this regard, but I want hon. members to know how concerned this group is about the moves the government is engaged in at this particular time. The brief states in part:
In a time of rapidly rising prices it is inconceivable for the government to remove this protective clause from low income earners who are struggling to maintain themselves and their families. The loss of 25 per cent of their original earnings is bad enough without the government knocking them even further down the economic ladder.
(Mr. Deputy Speaker.]
It seems to me the government is attempting to achieve restraint by taking $5 per week from these unemployed with dependants' earnings at a maximum of $3,200 per year only. That is when the circumstances are the most dire and the recipient could most use the money. In light of the fact that the new principle of unemployment insurance has been destroyed in any event by the government recognizing that sickness and pregnancy benefits should form part of unemployment insurance, then it seems to me that it is morally wrong at this time to remove this very small bit of protection for those who are with family, if you like, and who are counting on this amount of $5 a week.
In conclusion I would state it is wrong for the government to take from the poor-I do not say this lightly-and give to prisoners in order to bring about a facade in terms of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. These small reforms dealing with the aged and the poor mean nothing whatever. What should occur is that the government should move in an area whereby it can initiate policies that would bring about a satisfactory employment level. We will get into that later when it proposes to move the bench mark up to 5.6 per cent on an eight-year moving average.
This is where the government must move if it wants to make money. It must bring down the interest rate and bring down the eligibility period whereby someone can become eligible for unemployment insurance after being involved in the work force for a period of eight weeks. I would hope that as part of that experiment we will find a better way to deal with a bill in its last moments. The Fraser River Flood Control Agreement was signed on May 24, 1968, and at that time the estimated cost of the total program was $40 million and the cost to the federal government was $18 million. ing of the Fraser River diking project, consistent with approvals on this over-all program.
With probable financial constraints it will not be possible to provide complete protection to all parts of the valley, nor to correct inherent drainage problems in sparsely settled areas. Environmental factors are also important, and conservation of areas important to wild life and fisheries and fish habitat must take precedence in some areas in determining dike locations.
