It seems to me there are two classes of people that will be hit by this provision. First of all, there are those who cannot afford to retire at 65 from the labour force. It is true, as the minister has said, that they can get the Canada pension and old age security. If the spouse is over 60, then under the new provisions she will get financial assistance. But there are a great many people in the labour force today earning low wages, who have fairly large families, who have not been able to buy a house and who still have to pay high rent. These people cannot afford to drop out of the labour force. We will be saying to these people that if they continue to work they will not have any of the security, in times of periodic unemployment, that persons under 65 are able to enjoy.
I point out to the minister that in my constituency, for instance, men working in the lumber industry and in the forestry industries do seasonal work. They may be out of work for six or eight weeks when the snow closes up the logging camps. For this period of time this legislation will mean for them that they have no revenue at all from the unemployment insurance fund, despite the fact that they have paid into it for years. On the other hand, another individual who is two years younger will receive unemployment insurance. Both these people will go back to work when the logging camps reopen, one having had the benefit of unemployment insurance, the other not. I think this is a reprehensible discrimination against one group of individuals compared to another.
The second group of people that will be affected are those who do not want to retire because they have no particular hobby they want to follow and they are anxious to keep on working. Clause 10 of the bill will penalize these people. In a good many countries elderly people are encouraged to work. For instance, in Great Britain some of the factories now are hiring retired people for four hours a day. They have one shift in the forenoon and another in the afternoon. Their productivity has been comparable to that of workers of a younger age, and they have found that the psychotherapy that results has been excellent. Many of these people, Mr. Speaker, have worked all their lives: they have not learned how to play golf or to do any of the things people usually do when they retire. The fact that they have four hours of work a day and a little extra pay coming in means a great deal to them.
I took a group of people to Sweden some years ago and we spent a long time studying the labour market system in that country. What we are attempting in this amendment is to include also in that effective date of January 1, 1976, those clauses which add some manner of progressiveness to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The first of those is the extension of the qualifying period. We are in agreement with that. We feel that in respect of those who have been sick, or in some way disabled, this is a progressive clause which would extend the qualifying period so that they could go back two years to the time before they were so disabled or so taken sick. There was even a private member's bill from this side of the House in the name of the hon. member for Nickel Belt which would extend the qualifying period. So we admit this is a progressive move and feel that surely it should come into effect on January 1, 1976.
The other clause which we feel should come into effect on January 1, 1976, is the clause in respect of voluntary termination of a claim, which we believe is a progressive step. As we know there is no provision in the act for voluntary termination of a claim. It seems to me that clause 14 would provide this kind of a progressive move. It is a move that is long overdue. It should have been included in the act when it was brought in in 1971.
We also feel that clause 31 is a progressive move and that this clause should be included in the provisions of clause 38(2). This clause, which would provide for the payment of expenses of anyone appearing before the umpire, we believe is long overdue. Indeed we found out during the committee hearings that there were 40,000 appeals to the board of referees. In that same period only 400 appeals were made to the umpire. In other words one per cent of the appeals to the referees ended up as appeals to the umpire.
Certainly there must be a reason for such a low number of appeals going to the umpire. We suspect what the reason is. The minister has promised that a study is under way of the appeal procedures. One reason we do not think this section has been working to the advantage of the claimants is the fact that many of the claimants must travel long distances in order to appear before the umpire. We think that has been a disincentive to claimants. Therefore we

Speech:
It is wonderful what the Christmas spirit will do. One does hesitate at this stage of a session to raise a procedural argument, but rules are rules and it seems to me they should be observed.
I have in mind a rule that is frequently quoted and applied when members of the opposition seek to do what these amendments aim to do today. I hope, therefore, that the same strict application of the rule that is applied to opposition members of the House will be applied today to the government. The rule I have in mind stems from the rule of relevancy and, in particular, it gets down to this, that when there is before the House a bill that amends an act, it is clearly established that amendments to that amending bill must be relevant to the bill, must deal with matters that are in the bill. In other words, if one tries to put into an amending bill a clause that will have the effect of going behind the bill to the act itself, a clause that in effect tries to amend the act in particulars that are not before us, such amendments are out of order.
If I may go through the nine motions at one time, may I point out that motion No. 1 in the name of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) seeks to amend section 2 of the Public Service Superannuation Act.

This bill gives a female public servant the right to leave survivor benefits equal to those a male public servant can leave. From here on, female public servants will be paying for that right by contributing the same rate of premiums into the fund as a male public servant does. I said there was some urgency about this provision. This is because only those public servants who are in the public service, on strength, when this bill becomes law will be covered by it.
In other words, if a female public servant retired in Ottawa yesterday before the bill becomes law, she would not be covered. It would therefore be unfortunate if this bill were delayed in a way that would interfere with the rights of some who might be contemplating retirement, or who might be in a position where they have to retire very soon. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, that could have been avoided. All that was needed was to put in a bill a clause providing that, with respect to this so-called equality of status, there would be retroactivity to a certain date. This can still be done. The bill can still be rewritten and corrected in many ways to cover this point. As I say, that is one provision of the bill that has a certain element of urgency as well as being right, and we strongly support that part of the bill.

We then had to deal with it in the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations under pressure, because of the time element in regard to the one point I made, and perhaps in regard to one or two others.
In view of the request that has been made so often for other much needed improvements in public service superannuation, I think this has been a shabby way to treat us. I still think, with all the respect I have for the job done by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Francis), that the issues that were raised in committee were of such substance that we had the right to have the attendance of the President of the Treasury Board.
I want to say a few words about some of the points that are not dealt with in the bill that I think should be, the absence of which makes the bill unacceptable to us. I shall then speak about some of the matters in the bill which also make the bill unacceptable to us.
Allusions have been made to some of the matters I have in mind. I have already referred to the so-called equality of status in the bill, which is only equality to death. We feel that if there is going to be equality between men and women, their pensions ought to be equal. If a husband and wife live and work together and between them build up a certain pension right, what is there that is just about a law that provides a full pension so long as the man lives, but if he dies his widow gets only 50 per cent? If the woman dies first, the man who survives gets the full 100 per cent pension.
If the government is going to mouth this phrase about equality of status, we think it should go all the way and provide for equal pensions to the partners of a marriage where either one of them is employed in the public service. We raised this matter in the special joint committee, but of course we got the answer that it was beyond the terms of the Governor General's recommendation and could not be proceeded with for that reason. We were also told that it would be very costly. I recognize that, Mr. Speaker, but there are lots of things that are very costly which we can do in this place because we think they are right. I suggest that the phrase "equality of status" is a good phrase but that we really should put it into effect.

I do not accuse the government of any misleading language in the actual clauses of the bill. The title "equality of status" is there, but when it comes to the terms of the bill, what is meant is equality between male and female contributors, not equality between man and wife, between men and women in general terms. We regret very much that the government has not seen fit to move in the direction of equality of status in real terms so far as men and women are concerned, and this failure makes the bill very unacceptable to us. Mr. Speaker, I am going to be very brief with my remarks respecting Bill C-20, as I know there are one or two others who would like to speak before six o'clock.
I am in favour of this bill in general principle as indeed I believe are most members. I like the idea of the waiting period for citizenship being reduced from five years to three years. This move is long overdue and I welcome it.
The age of majority will be reduced from 21 years to 18 years. This is a logical step because the age of majority for Canadian citizens in all provinces I believe, and certainly federally, is 18 years.
Men and women are finally to be treated equally. It was a sad commentary on the old Citizenship Act that they were not. Now, for example, children born abroad will derive citizenship from either parent. At the present time a child acquires Canadian citizenship only if the father is Canadian.
Another example is that all applicants for Canadian citizenship will be required to meet the three year residence qualification without regard to marital connection with a citizen. Under the present act only one year of residence is required for the alien wife of a Canadian citizen. The act is certainly bringing into reality in law what has been the actual practice and I am happy about those changes.
British subjects will no longer be exempt from the requirement to be examined by a citizenship judge or to attend a citizenship ceremony. I happen to be only half Canadian as my father was born in England. In my constituency there are a lot of persons of Anglo-Saxon background who are touchy about the fact that some of their traditional so-called rights are being infringed upon. I say frankly, openly, and honestly that I do not know why we should continue giving any special exemption to immigrants from the United Kingdom when those same rights are not given to immigrants from other countries. I am prepared to meet criticism from people of Anglo-Saxon origin in my constituency, and I think this bill is fair to all ethnic groups entering the country.

January 27, 1976
Citizenship
The removal of the discrimination against women is certainly in line with the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. This has been long in coming but I am happy that it has finally arrived in Bill C-20.
The reduction in the eligibility age makes sense since the voting age is now 18. Some people have argued that this provision should have been introduced under the Elections Act. That is a moot point which I will not belabour. In effect this changes things after the fact and this argument has been made previously.
The period of residence required prior to application for citizenship is another important change. It seems obvious that the present five year wait was an arbitrary decision, as indeed is the proposed three year wait. I do not know how we would arrive at the correct figure, whether it be one year, two, three, four, or five, but certainly the reduction is a step in the right direction.
The five year period was probably imposed because very often the wives of immigrants who stayed home to raise their families did not get out into the work force, or out of the home, and so found it difficult to pick up the language. I do not think this should be an obstacle. In cases that I am familiar with, the wives do try their best to communicate, particularly those from eastern Europe or the Mediterranean countries from where most of our immigrants now come. If their children are learning English or French and their husbands are speaking English or French, I do not think they should be held back.

I think he has every right to be complimentary, particularly when we compare our system of paying for medical services and hospital services with the way in which such services are paid for in the United States.
Recently during the Christmas season a senior public servant, in the employment of the federal government, with his family visited a large city in the United States. One of his children became sick and had to be admitted to hospital. The family was told that the child would not be ' admitted to the hospital until they had first deposited a cheque in the amount of $1,500 with the hospital in order to take care of possible and probable hospital costs. It is a long time since any Canadian citizen had to face that kind of situation in this country, and we can thank the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) who instituted the hospital insurance plan in Saskatchewan when he was premier, and the federal Conservative government which extended that plan to all the provinces in Canada, and also the federal Liberal government which, taking the example of the province of Saskatchewan, began a medical insurance plan paid for by the federal and provincial governments.
What the minister is proposing is what he first proposed in 1973, that is, that 50 per cent of the cost of medical insurance paid for by the federal government would no longer be paid but rather that on a declining scale the amount paid by the federal government would be capped, that a limit would be put on the increase paid by the federal government of 14 per cent in 1976-1977, of 10 per cent 1977-1978, and of a smaller amount, to be negotiated with the provinces, for future years.

refusing to pay 50 per cent of the cost as it has until now and, secondly, to the federal government deciding unilaterally that it would reduce the percentage which it paid.
Let us remember that many of the provinces ,did not want to become involved in a universal government sponsored, government operated medical insurance plan. If my memory serves me correctly, the province of Ontario with its Conservative government was the last province to join the medical insurance plan. They did not want to join that plan because they believed that the former voluntary plan was adequate and that all that a government should do is to pay the premiums for those people who cannot afford to be covered under the voluntary plans. February 2, 1976
Adjournment Debate
access to the United States market for our Canadian beef and veal. This was suggested the day before the minister went to Washington to confer with U.S. secretary of agriculture, Mr. Butz, on the egg issue and beef and veal quotas.
My suggestion was both kindly and logical in view of the recent strained relationship between our two countries over the cattle and beef trade and quotas in the last year and a half.
I also suggested that if cattle and beef quotas were to be renegotiated, they should be at or near historical trade levels, similar to Canada's five year average pattern, instead of a 12 month August to August quota as used by the U.S.
The minister's response was a very cynical and sarcastic comment that he would do nothing to offend the CCA because they do not want government interference. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that good, sound, properly negotiated bilateral trade arrangements do not constitute government interference.
Just two days before my question the minister had invited the CCA executive to meet with him and his senior staff to discuss this matter, as well as the current stabilization issue. While I can commend the minister for this action in asking the CCA for comments and advice, I must report that due to the constraints resulting from the Agricultural Outlook Conference which took place at the same time, it was not a fruitful meeting. The minister just did not arrange sufficient time for this special meeting called at his request.
Nevertheless, it is rather interesting to note the developments of the minister's meeting with Mr. Butz as reported in the minister's press release dated December 31. The release announced the end of beef quotas on December 31 by both countries, and reminded us that live cattle quotas had been lifted last August. The statement went on to report:
"During our meeting, Mr. Butz pointed out that the U.S. have a meat import law in their statutes and they must operate under it" Mr. Whelan said.
"Taking that into account, I advised Mr. Butz that Canada would need to provide similar safeguards to protect against any unusual or excessive meat flow into this country.
"We have reached agreement in this context and are very satisfied with the arrangement".
Toward the end of the press release we find the following:
Mr. Whelan also noted the agreement opens the way for discussions with Australia and New Zealand.
"These two countries are significant exporters of beef to Canada. We have already advised both countries that we want to make similar arrangements with them to ensure orderly marketing", Mr. Whelan said.
While the minister did not use the term "Canadian meat import law" his phrase "similar safeguards" does indeed suggest that he was aware of the cattlemen's views, and CCA, I am sure, would like to see this suggestion further developed between Canada and the U.S.A., and between Canada and Australia and New Zealand. I am sure he would like to ensure that never again will we in Canada have to endure a flood of U.S. cattle which collapsed our

markets, such as in the summer of 1973 following the U.S. price control program.
In the cattle industry we in Canada share with the U.S. cattle producers the North American beef market together with Mexico, of course. These three countries are indeed partners in the North American beef economy, but we are not equal partners. With a ten to one ratio of both people and cattle populations as between USA and Canada it is obvious that the U.S. market dominates the north American cattle and beef market, and therefore has much greater capacity either to benefit or damage our Canadian market, and both of these situations have occurred. Let me make it abundantly clear at this point that I fully support the concept that our Canadian cattle industry should continue to be a vital part of the north American cattle market.

It is undefinable and does not exist in the context the government claims in the legislation before us. When we think in terms of percentage, we must realize that we are using a mathematical concept. We are dealing with units or numbers.
It is possible to talk about percentage if we are talking about volume, length, weight, or anything for which we can use a unit of measurement. If we talk about miles, centimetres, kilograms, pounds or anything which is a unit of measurement, we can use the term 80 per cent, but I challenge hon. members opposite, and the minister specifically, to tell us the unit of measurement used with regard to censoring a foreign magazine.

We challenged him by asking if we took a piece of material which was 100 column inches long and reduced it to 20 inches, but it really had the same content material in it, would that be acceptable under the regulation of the government, and he responded, yes. However, the minister interjected and said no, it must be substantially different in content.
The hon. member for Sault Ste Marie (Mr. Symes) said that the government is not into a censorship program. I suggest that it is because if it is saying that the content must be substantially different and it cannot define the unit of measurement, it is a case of the government making

the decision and being the judge. The fact of the matter is that this government does not know what the unit of measurement is. It is applying a mathematical concept to a value judgment, which is impossible.
If we are going to talk about a situation in which foreign publications or foreign material comes into this country to be printed and is subjected to a bureaucratic value judgment we must recognize, that as a subjective position, that does not have a unit of measurement. It cannot be measured in percentages-that can only be applied when we speak of weight, length, or volume. We cannot apply percentages to value judgments. That is the central point of Bill C-58, whether or not his brainwashed officials want to think of it in another way. The point I am making is that it is not immoral to receive revenues for services rendered. We cannot say that the U.S. stations are doing something wrong when they sell in Canada, when for many years-more years than the U.S. stations-we have been, and still are, doing the same thing in reverse; in other words, selling from a Canadian market into a major U.S. market.

lawyers in Washington, D C., who are attorneys specializing in broadcasting law, I can state specifically that Canadian signals are treated in exactly the same way as U.S. signals, with no exception anywhere in the United States. By this I mean that, instead of calling a signal either a domestic or a foreign signal, the designation is either a local or a distant signal. Because Canadian signals are not located in a U.S. city, they are designated as distant signals, but they receive the same treatment as distant U.S. signals.
If I were a U.S. border station, all I could ask of the Canadian government in terms of taxes, and of the Canadian cable system in terms of carrying my signal, would be that they do exactly the same to me as their U.S. counterparts do to Canadian signals. When we get into broadcasting I want to say something about the fact that the finest channel coming into the lower mainland is not a Canadian channel. It is American channel 9 out of Seattle. It is an educational channel. Again those of us in this House who do not support the amendment also do not support the idea that existing programming should be deleted from the cable.
There is every reason to have full choice in the lower mainland of British Columbia. In fact if we stop thinking of just today's debate and think ahead a little, a converter before long will become standard equipment on television sets. We will go to 36 channels in the foreseeable future, within a few years, and this will provide us with all the variety of programming we need. Commercial programming fulfils a responsibility all right but it does not fulfil the democratic need for variety of programming because stations are at the whim of the advertiser.
Without proper ratings all you can appeal to is either the lowest common denominator or the largest audience. But there is a significant audience out there for something different than Mary Tyler Moore three times a week, plus re-runs, or "I Love Lucy". We will have a chance to reach
Non-Canadian Publications
all those different audiences under the converter system. We do not need to be narrow about allowing American programs on to the cable system. We could cope with all of them, including a French station in Vancouver, and we could expand our service into areas which do not normally share in television.
Let's have an original play once in a while. Let's have a little educational television which we have not had for a very long time. That is why I want to mention once again channel 9, a public service channel out of Seattle which has used some CBC programming too, because it seems to me to be satisfying an audience which is very unhappy with commercial television programming. I remember when Sunday mornings used to be called a television ghetto hour, when we had a few public discussions and something worth-while in terms of satisfying the intellect. That is gone, because if programs do not measure up under the rating system advertisers will not touch them with a ten foot pole.
As I see it one of the main functions of public broadcasting is to extend to everyone a variety of choice. Then we can protect Canadian nationalism. We do not need to shut off the border or to blank out signals from a certain direction. Nevertheless it is important that we support stations within our own borders, particularly in terms of revenue, and this is the objective of Bill C-58.
As I say, we cannot support the amendment that has been put forward. Television station KVOS is to some extent an innocent victim of this legislation, but we really do not have a solution to the problem. In fact there is no solution for KVOS because it is an FCC licensed station in the Bellingham area. I would be pleased to see them given a CRTC licence and establish themselves in Vancouver so they can go into production with revenues from the Vancouver area. That would be satisfactory. But since it is not licensed for the Vancouver area it is not really under the jurisdiction of the CRTC. I therefore submit the amendment before us should not be supported.

Park personnel are available to visit local organizations and present programs about the Park. measure of whose design is individual profit or punishment.

My feelings about nationalism and ... prejudices against it lie in the very history and meaning of the word. I never thought the nation should have preponderance over the individual...

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Faulkner) has been assured by the Registrar of Citizenship that the citizenship applications and certifi-
February 24, 1976

cate presentations in the Toronto area have been carefully looked into as a result of the hon. member's question. He has further been informed that the backlog alluded to is not as serious as suggested.
As an example and with reference to the St. Clair citizenship court, there were only 581 certificates on hand as of February 12, all of which will have been presented by February 26. For the information of this House it should be known that this particular citizenship court now has a scheduling whereby certificates are presented within 14 days of receipt from Ottawa. The 14 days in question are used for scheduling the ceremonies and informing the applicants.
With reference to the Dufferin court it had, as of February 12, some 726 certificates on hand, 400 of which will be distributed this month. Although another 300 certificates will have been received for presentation before the end of the month, this is not an unduly large number of certificates to have on hand in courts as large as the two to which I have referred.
In 1975, through our Toronto courts' system only, a total of over 49,000 grants of citizenship were made. This figure includes those grants made through storefront offices, the mobile team, and the subcourts in Oshawa, Brampton and Barrie. In addition to the large number of grants of citizenship processed by the Toronto citizenship court system, there were 36,391 proofs of citizenship given out in 1975. These proofs do not, of course, involve a court ceremony and presentation but nevertheless account for a large volume of work by court personnel.
I would also like to take the opportunity to say a word about the success of the citizenship outreach program, since I believe it has a bearing on the questions raised by the hon. member. The storefront concept was introduced in Toronto in July 1973, which means there have been two and a half years of storefront operation.
In 1975 there were 13,420 storefront grant applications, an increase of 21 per cent over the previous year. There were almost 4,000 proof applications processed in the storefront offices, a percentage increase of 53 per cent. There would seem, however, to be no need at the present time to increase staff in the Toronto court system beyond the filling of existing vacancies.
The effect of the outreach program has been to relieve the overburdened situation at the St. Clair office which, until 1973, was the only citizenship registration office in Toronto. With the opening of the Dufferin court in July, 1975, and with the outreach services provided by storefront and mobile operations, grants volume in the St. Clair court decreased by 10 per cent in 1975.
With respect to citizenship hearings, no backlog exists vis-a-vis the St. Clair court. There is, however, a one-month delay at the Dufferin court which involves approximately 600 applications. A delay in hearings also exists at Barrie and Brampton involving approximately 250 applicants. This situation will be corrected when a new citizenship judge is appointed.

BasePK: 3014660

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked if the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) had been made aware of complaints concerning the inadequate French language television coverage of the Progressive Conservative convention and if it was the intention of the minister to remind the publicly financed Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of its primary responsibility to report in both official languages all public affairs of national interest. The minister replied that the corporation had a responsibility to report important events in both official languages on both channels.
Last Thursday the hon. member for Cumberland-Col-chester North (Mr. Coates) expressed his dissatisfaction with programmed CBC radio coverage in his area.
Earlier today the hon. member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) proposed, by way of a motion under Standing Order 43, to refer the subject to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts. The motion required unanimous consent which, unfortunately, was not forthcoming. I say unfortunately, because it is my opinion that a dissenting voice came from among the members of the party that was considerably disenchanted with the treatment accorded that party by the publicly owned television network.
During the question period today a member of the official opposition, I believe the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), again raised the subject of inadequate French language television coverage of the Progressive Conservative convention. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Miss Campbell) replied, giving information supplied by the CBC and which, in my opinion, was no answer at all. It was a reiteration of what programming there was and did not answer the question.
We are already aware of the amount of coverage accorded by the French network of the CBC. As Joan Irwin stated so well in an article in yesterday's Montreal Gazette, and I quote:
Both English networks made a major commitment to the Canadian public by providing an opportunity to participate in an important political event. They deserve our gratitude.
French-speaking Canadians, on the other hand, had almost no opportunity to acquaint themselves with the PC leadership candidates or with the political philosophies of a major national party at a crucial moment in its history.
It's not particularly surprising that TeleMetropole and the TVA network ignored the whole thing until the results of the voting were known.
It is surprising and entirely indefensible that the CBC French network showed so little interest in the convention or in the rights of its audience to be well informed on vital national issues.
Radio-Canada carried none of Saturday's convention live during the speeches of the 12 leadership candidates, despite the fact that three candidates were from Quebec-and two of them front-runners for the leadership.
Not until 11:10 p.m. (after the hockey game and the news) did Radio-Canada give its audience a glimpse of the convention, and then only in edited bits of each candidate's speech-of which many were poorly translated by an extremely uncertain male translator.

February 24, 1976
Adjournment Debate
On Sunday, Radio-Canada had intended to devote only the six to eight p.m. period to the convention. Then it said it would begin its coverage at four p.m.
Finally someone in the French network saw the light, and it was announced that Sunday's coverage would begin at 2:30 p.m.
The indecision and irresponsibility of the French network indicate an alarming narrowness of view and curious perception of the tax-supported corporation's obligations to the Canadian public-all the Canadian public.
The estimates have now been tabled. Included in those of the Secretary of State is the sum of $416 million for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, an increase over last year for operating expenditures alone of over $50 million.
Whenever I question the present Secretary of State, and also when I questioned his predecessor, I was lectured on independence and the inability of the Secretary of State to interfere. They argue that they have no legal right to meddle in the affairs on an independent corporation. Well, I have news for the Secretary of State. As long as taxpayers in my constituency see vast sums of their tax moneys being poured into a corporation which services only an average 11 per cent of the population, they are going to be on my back, and rightly so. In turn, I am going to expect the Secretary of State to come up with answers.
I am sure the minister will not forget the political indiscretion that I committed in 1973 by proposing in committee a nominal cut in the estimates to indicate that the politician still had some say in the publicly financed CBC. That motion passed with the help of some of my more experienced colleagues. Whilst I may not take such a step again, I do want to point out that there must be some established line of communication between those who spend the money and those who are responsible for paying the bills.
The Progressive Conservative party may not be strong in its parliamentary representation from Quebec, but its total
percentage vote in that province is healthy. However, apart from that party's supporters, there were those from all other parties and those with no political affiliation who wanted to watch the convention proceedings.
The English coverage extended over four days. It was generally well handled. Why were French Canadians shafted by the television channel which owes its very existence to the considerable financial support of the taxpayer; as I said earlier, $416 million?
May I request that an inquiry be instituted and a full statement made to all members of this House on this continuing saga of complete irresponsibility.

I have no grudge against chain stores but I want to point particularly at the manufacturers who supply those chain stores, when they put ads in papers which mislead the consumer by offering him a $60 tire for $23 or $24 and alleging that it is of the same size and the same quality as the $60 one.

Mr. Speaker, just before one o'clock I rose to respond to the comments of the two hon. gentlemen who spoke between twelve and one o'clock, in the hope of allaying their reservations about clause 8 of Bill C-61.
March 5, 1976

First, however, may I thank the House for allowing last evening a procedural modification which will facilitate the consideration of Bill C-61. In error, we had grouped motions 1, 2 and 3 together for discussion, whereas motions 1 and 5 and 2 and 3 ought to have been grouped together for discussion. May I extend my thanks to the House, to the Chair and to the Table for their assistance in this, which will help in the consideration of this bill.
Last evening hon. members commented about the brevity of my remarks at the beginning of the report stage, and about the minister's absence. Let me make two points. First, my initial comments dealt only with the technical accuracy of the French version of a particular clause vis-avis the English version. That concerned motions 1 and 5. I am happy to see the confusion on that point resolved. I did not mean to imply last evening that I had nothing else to say about the other substantive portions of the bill. I welcome today's opportunity to comment more extensively on substantive aspects of this legislation and proposed amendments to it.
Hon. members also commented last evening on the minister's inability to be present. Let me explain why the minister was unable to be present when we began the report stage discussion. The minister was in the House yesterday until late afternoon waiting for Bill C-61 to be called. It was called only late in the day, unfortunately after he had been called away on business. Any inference to the contrary is misleading. I think it important to indicate the reason for the minister's absence. To those hon. members who want an assurance, I am able to say that the minister intends to participate in this debate. He would have done so last evening if he could have been present. He will at the first opportunity during our consideration of Bill C-61, address himself specifically to concerns which hon. members and people outside the House have voiced about various aspects of the bill.
It is apparent that the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), in whose name stands motion No. 2, and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), in whose name stands motion No. 3, are concerned about the provisions of clause 8. As has been mentioned, clause 8 involves the basic principles of the Canadian coasting trade. The establishment of such provisions for Canada is, in the opinion of many in this House and outside, long overdue. The hon. member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich argue that clause 8 is not strong enough, should be tightened or strengthened or made to speak more loudly, if I may say this. Meanwhile, other hon. members opposite are not so sure. Last evening the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) went so far as to say that in his opinion clause 8 should be deleted from the bill altogether. I draw attention to that point not only to illustrate differences of opinion or a division of view among members opposite, but it also illustrates the complexity, delicacy and fundamental importance of coasting trade provisions and of the general question of the coasting trade with which clause 8 deals.
That question is not to be easily, neatly and simply resolved. The issues on both sides of the question are of concern to the government. Having consulted the industry, labour, professional groups, provincial governments and
Maritime Code
others interested, we have tried to meet the problem. The result is this bill. I trust that in the final analysis all the work undertaken in the attempt to reach an accommodation will bear fruit.
Dealing specifically with the second motion on the order paper standing in the name of the hon. member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East, I want to assure him that the concern he has raised is not an issue which has escaped the attention of the government or the draftsmen who did the technical work in putting the legislation together.
There is a good argument that relates more particularly to the next motion that also applies here. The wording as presently drawn in general terms covers the situation adequately. The hon. member argued in committee, and I believe in the House, that it would not be an uncommon step for us to give the governor in council the power to make a declaration from time to time that a certain foreign area, territory, port or place would be deemed to be a part of Canada. It may not be an unprecedented move to do that, but it is an unusual step, particularly in the terms in which this amendment is phrased; that is, virtually giving to the governor in council the authority to declare a foreign territory in its entirety to be a part of Canada. That is a fairly extreme and drastic power.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) introduced this guillotine motion he said he did so with reluctance. And well he might. Not only should he have a feeling of reluctance; he ought to be ashamed at introducing a motion relating to a matter on which only about one quarter of the members of this House have spoken and which has far-reaching consequences for the people of Canada.
[Mr. Hnatyshyn.l
What we ought to ask ourselves is why this closure motion is being introduced. It is being introduced to enable the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to sit down and negotiate with the provincial ministers of health with a loaded gun on the table. As a matter of fact, there will be two loaded guns. The first gun will be the termination notice that the government issued last June with respect to its contributions to hospital insurance. The second loaded gun will be Bill C-68, which is to limit the contribution that the federal government will make to national medicare.
The government is anxious to get this bill through second reading so that when the provincial ministers of health meet with the federal representatives this legislation will have passed at least through second reading and the minister will be able to say to his provincial conter-parts, "Parliament has approved our position; you can either take it or leave it".
I think it is important, Mr. Speaker, to look at the sequence of events which have taken place and the moves which the Minister of National Health and Welfare has made to avoid meeting the provincial ministers of health until he has this legislation through second reading. Let me remind the House that in May of 1973 the federal government proposed to the provincial governments that the federal government's contribution to medicare should be tied to the gross national product. We have only to look at what happened to the gross national product last year to realize what would happen if the provinces accepted that proposal. But in September of 1974 the provinces unanimously rejected the proposal. They not only rejected the proposal, they made an alternative proposal. They said, "We can help save money both for the federal and the provincial governments by having lower cost services, and we are prepared to sit down and discuss that".
At the last federal-provincial health ministers' conference in January, 1975, the Minister of National Health and Welfare agreed with the provincial representatives that this was the best way to go about cutting down costs both with regard to hospital insurance and medicare. As the minister admitted in the House on January 28 of this year, it was agreed that officials of both the federal government and the provincial governments were authorized to get together to begin working out programs by which lower cost services would be introduced, thereby eliminating many of the high cost services. That was a good arrangement, one that was entered into in good faith by both the provinces and the federal government.
On June 23 last the federal government pulled the rug from under these arrangements by announcing in the budget of the minister of finance, first that it would give a termination notice with regard to hospital insurance, and second, that it would introduce the measures contained in Bill C-68 to put a cap on the federal government's contribution to medicare.
The provinces were aghast. They felt they had been cheated and betrayed and they discontinued discussions. They felt there was no value in holding discussions in view of the two decisions that the federal government announced in the minister of finance's budget. I do not wonder that the provinces are outraged.

March 11, 1976

The fact of the matter is, it is the area of the private members' bill to propose legislative enactment by this House which relieves individuals from the operations of existing statutes. An example is bills to relieve operations of the Criminal Code with respect to penalties and jail terms vis-a-vis persons imprisoned under the general law. It has been held that if it is the effect of a bill to exempt an individual from the operation of the general law, it is a proper subject matter for a private right and public bill. Since this is a private bill, one would have to make the corollary, if it does establish an exemption with respect to the general law, that it must be taken to be within the purview of a private bill.
Whether that is a desirable objective is a matter for debate and division. After extensive discussion and consideration, I think that motion No. 1 ought to be put and considered for discussion and division forthwith.

Motion No. 1.

However, at this time I should like to lay before the House my bias in this connection. I have found that banks and trust companies are the least desireble institutions to which an individual, a private person, should go in order to obtain a loan. Bill S-30 is designed to establish a new bank which will convert the assets of IAC Limited into its operation. I notice that the company chose first to introduce this bill in the Senate in the hope, quite understandably, it would receive a much more positive reception there because of the number of Senators who have an interest in banks. Indeed the bill was quite speedily approved there.
I think it is important that this House should examine a little more closely the bill which is before us. We should consider the dangerous precedent involved in allowing a finance institution such as this to avoid the carefully thought out provisions and safeguards contained in the Bank Act of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I see it is six o'clock. May I call it six o'clock at this time.

The only way that small secondary industry is going to get ahead in Canada is if it receives the support in many cases of the federal government. A case in point was brought out by my question of December 12, 1975, when I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), and I quote:
Because of the comparative advantage we enjoy in the ceramics industry in Canada-
I am not so sure we can maintain this advantage if the government keeps acting in the manner it did with regard to the Calgary airport contract.
-will the minister, together with the Minister of Supply and Services and Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, assure this industry that government contracts will specify the use of available Canadian ceramic products and that we will not follow the practice followed in the case of the new Calgary airport?
The minister replied that the government observes some broad rules-and I emphasize the word broad-in connection with Canadian materials. He continued:
I do not know if they apply in the particular case in question, or to a specific tendering operation, but I will look into the matter.
The case I am referring to concerned the letting of tenders for ceramic tile for the new airport at Calgary. The specifications stated a Canadian tile should be used. Canadian tile and German tile were tested by the Alberta Research Council; both were deficient in some areas, but the German tile had more deficiencies. Then it was brought to the attention of the government that the specifications were more stringent than Canadian government specifications board standard No. 75-GP-1B. Subsequently, the tenders were issued on the revised specifications to which Canadian tile could subscribe. Tenders were submitted; Frontenac Tile and International Brick and Tile, both Canadian companies, and a Germany company submitted quotations, and International Brick and Tile was the lowest Canadian bid.
The architect stated he wanted German tile because he was familiar with it and would guarantee it. But the Research Council of Alberta had done extensive study and tests on Alberta tile, and had in fact helped set up the process and kilns and was prepared to stand behind it. The province of Alberta's minister of transport was prepared to give assurances as to the ability to deliver on time and would give written guarantees. Federal people on site
March 11, 1976

seemed satisfied at the time. However, after all these assurances the government gave the contract to a German company and based its decision on the uncertainty of deliverability. Unreal, Mr. Speaker!
I can only say that I hope that after the minister looks into this situation he will see that this does not happen again. There were some labour and farmer and socialist groups in various parts of the country which were the forerunners of our movement, but I think that any objective student of history, including any of us, would have to agree that the progressive element in Canadian politics was represented by what the Liberal convention fought and stood for in 1919.

Some of the things in it were already common practice in democratic countries of western Europe and some other parts of the world, but they were not yet here in Canada so the Liberal party took its stand for a whole host of progressive measures in the social and labour fields.
It is true that if you read through this document you will find a lot of hoopla in it, though not quite as lively as the hoopla of modern conventions. You will find a lot of condemning of the government in power, and a lot of passing the buck and all of that. But I say quite categorically, Mr. Speaker, that the commitment the Liberals made in 1919 to try to move this country forward was quite noteworthy.
Included in the list of things that the Liberal party committed itself to in 1919, as set out in the resolution moved by Mackenzie King, was a commitment to old age pensions, unemployment insurance, and health insurance. One might have hoped, of course, that since that party got into power a couple of years later it would not have taken long until those objectives were realized. But even the progressive Liberals of the 1920's were pretty slow moving. It actually took more than 40 years to get the Liberals to come through with all the things they had promised in that great convention of 1919.
During those 40 years or more there had to be an awful lot of prodding from this side of the House. Our forerunners in the persons of Mr. Woodsworth, Miss Agnes Mac-Phail and Mr. Heaps had to get here. The C.C.F. had to come along, and then the NDP, to prod all these things. I think it is fair to suggest that over those 40 or 50 years the Liberal party did move in the direction of social legislation for the good of Canada.

The question of a public inquiry opens problems for parliament and the judiciary which seem to me to be difficult in the extreme. Since parliament should zealously guard its privileges, any such inquiry involving its own members or members of the judiciary should necessarily be by a committee of parliament. If the misdemeanour lies with a judge, that is a parliamentary responsibility. If the misdemeanour is that of a member of parliament or minister responsible to parliament, that matter also must be heard by parliament.
Clearly, parliament would not wish to delegate this fundamental task to an outside body. We might thus have a committee of parliament conducting an inquisitorial investigation of what ministers might have said to ministers, what ministers might have said to judges, what judges might have said to judges, what judges might have said to lawyers, what lawyers acting for judges might have said to newspaper reporters, and so on, and on, and on. Even if parliament were to delegate the function to an outside appointed tribunal of inquiry, the same features would exist. Surely those wishing to maintain public respect for the independence of the judiciary would not welcome such a form of inquisition.

Mr. Speaker, I am that much happier to take part in the debate on this motion that it is so definitely realistic that it deals with so actual a subject that it contrasts with the issue previously discussed, namely the question of privilege which delayed our proceedings by almost two hours.
Mr. Speaker, after having heard the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), we must, above all, refrain from closing our eyes and see the situation as it is. I feel it is appropriate at this point that we should consider the factors which brought about the situation in which our industrial milk producers now find themselves. If the minister feels, as he has just shown, that there are no solutions, that the problems cannot be overcome, for the very same reasons we have been hearing for years, and year after year, we must come to one of two conclusions: either the government is not progressing at all, or it has no idea whatsoever of what progress is; and I would even go further and prove right then and there that the minister is not aware of the situation.
The government is criticized for allowing into this country products that can easily be manufactured in Canada in adequate quantities. The minister referred to that a moment ago; he said the Canadian Dairy Commission, in co-operation with his department is preventing the importation of butter; yes, he said that, barely five or ten minutes ago. But, on the other hand, import permits are being issued. Where is the logic in that? Imports are forbidden but permits are issued. I have proof if it here. This is a country where producers are penalized for producing over and above their quotas, while importation is allowed! I have here a question asked by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) which is on the Order Paper. I quote:
1.	Did Canada import butter in the first eight months of 1974 and, if so, a) how many pounds of butter were imported, b) during what months?
2.	a) From what countries was it imported, b) what quantities were imported from each country, c) at what cost per pound?
I hope the minister will not tell me again that butter is not imported.

Mr. Speaker, if I offended one of my colleagues by naming him, it is because I got carried away. Perhaps I have too much at heart the matter before the House today. I want to single out the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) and I can say that he is really sincere. I often saw him at the sittings of the committee on agriculture and if he is ill today, I wish him a speedy recovery. I can say he is really devoted to agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether we should go witchhunting and find out who is the villain, or whether we should not work together to find a solution to this problem. [English]
I think we could gain much from working together, approaching this problem in a co-operative manner, and everyone concerned accepting part of the blame, the Canadian Dairy Commission, the marketing boards, the Producers' Association, the producers themselves, the excellent weather we had last year, and perhaps we should also blame the cows for giving too much milk. I sense the feeling in our discussions with the producers that they all agree there was a surplus in production and they all agree to reduce production this year.
When we asked the producers to reduce their production, they agreed to the tune of some 10 per cent, 15 per cent, and for some of them, perhaps 20 per cent. That will mean a
March 19, 1976

gross revenue minus of some 10 per cent or 15 per cent, but when it comes to a net revenue, that will mean something in the vicinity of 25 per cent or 30 per cent less for them. This we cannot accept, and that is why we have made strong recommendations to our cabinet and strong recommendations to the Treasury Board.
Since I suggest we are responsible for the surplus on hand, and the producers agreed to reduced incomes, I also suggest that the cabinet consider our working paper which was presented so that the government will take its share of the blame. The dairy commission should also accept its part of the blame and during this coming year monitor the production on a much more precise and regular basis, and report to the government and to the marketing agencies so that the over production of this year will not be repeated. [Translation]
Of course, this would be done with the co-operation of the management committees who are also parity responsible because they are in charge of marketing.
In his motion, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) refers to a long term policy. I would appreciate it if he would follow more closely the discussions on agriculture and the changes effected in the dairy industry. In my humble opinion, as long as we have two markets for a single production, there will be some confusion and it will be practically impossible to implement a long term policy. It will be possible as soon as all our producers are integrated. It is quite difficult to understand an integration system for those of us who are not farmers. A cow has four teats, two connectd to the industrial milk tube and two on the whole milk tube, and it is rather difficult to explain the price margin to consumers. During the few months I have attended their meetings in the three years I have spent here, those matters have been explained to me. Now I understand that whole milk producers have incurred more expenditures. If eventually total integration in carried out, the producers will be refunded the extra expenditures they incurred on their farm.
It is our fondest wish to see along term policy established for the dairy industry, but as I said earlier, I suggest that there should be a single market for a dairy product. Then a long term policy would be feasible.
I am convinced, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said earlier, that if workers in other sectors were as productive as those in the agricultural sector, and I would even point out to the President of the Treasury Board that if his public servants were as effective as our farmers, we would have a lot more services, and perhaps our production and service costs would be reduced here in Canada.
I will conclude by saying that I have read a press report about a provincial minister criticizing the federal government. I would instead invite him to join with the federal minister in trying together to develop a policy that will help farmers rather than hurt them.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North was mistaken in one respect. Much in his address was worth while, but I think there was a certain misconception of the original and fundamental purpose of the Senate. He spoke of the fact that second chambers around the world are disappearing. That is true, of course, but it is not true that they are disappearing in federal systems. In federal systems the role of second chambers is as strong as ever. That, of course, is the principal justification for having a Senate in Canada. It is not merely for the sober second thought, the review by an upper house, with presumably more time and, some might claim, more ability to review the decisions of this House; the more important point is the fact that in the Senate we have representation by region-representation which can give acknowledgement to interests of various parts of the country that would not occur on a strictly representation-by-population basis.
The hon. member quoted Sir John A. Macdonald and his views on the origin of the Senate. I think it is worth-while putting on record the views of the famous Grit of that day, the Hon. George Brown. Speaking in the debates in the House of Assembly in 1865 after the resolutions that had their genesis in Charlottetown and which subsequently were approved in Quebec, he said:
The very essence of our compact is that the union shall be federal and not legislative. Our Lower Canada friends have agreed to give us representation by population in the Lower House, on the express condition that they shall have equality in the Upper House. On no other condition could we have advanced a step-
I think it is clear in the viewpoint of George Brown-[DOT] and it is the viewpoint of most historians today that this was one of the crucial steps toward confederation-that in the Upper House representation would be on the basis of region and that would give protection to the maritimes and to Quebec which would not otherwise be there.
Parenthetically, it is rather unusual for a federal union to have representation on the basis of a whole region. I believe in all the other federal systems where there are upper houses, which I think is about all of them, representation is on the basis of the constituent governmental unit; that is, on the basis of the province or state rather than on the basis of region. In Canada it is only in the case of Ontario and Quebec, and I believe Newfoundland, that we have representation on that basis; for other provinces it is a regional concept.
I think it is important to understand that our purpose in having a Senate is primarily that of protecting regional interests and not of reviewing legislation already adopted by this House. Occasionally it is true the Senate makes a real contribution to the legislation passed by this House by way of correcting it in matters of detail. For example, there may be revisions made by the Senate to one of our pieces of legislation which will be coming back to this House for reconsideration. I do not think anyone would deny that in matters of this kind the Senate can make a real contribution.
In wider investigations in recent years the Senate has also proved itself to be extremely valuable to our political system. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North mentioned, Senator Croll has been particularly prominent in leading several Senate committees to reports which have been of great value in the subject areas with which they

dealt. Further, with respect to certain bills which have been introduced in this House and have not been introduced in the Senate, the Senate has held hearings at the same time as ours which have enabled them to proceed with the bill more quickly later, and, in the case of income tax legislation, they have been able to provide helpful suggestions. There are also cases where legislation which has not yet been introduced in this House has been introduced in the Senate, and as a result of Senate consideration it has been decided by the government that there are great areas of the act which should be changed. I think of matters like the new bankruptcy legislation where the Senate investigation last year proved so valuable to the government and to this House.
The Senate does, then, make a real contribution to the legislative process, but I think we would all regard it as intolerable if the Senate were to set itself up in an undemocratic fashion to try to determine by a second look what members of this House should be passing as legislation. After all, we are the people elected by the citizens of Canada-by those who have the right to vote in Canada- to determine what the policies and laws of this country should be. We could not accept any challenge from an appointed Senate on this point.
This accounts for the fact that in 1973 or 1974, when a change was made by the Senate to the wiretapping legislation passed by this House, legislation which was the result of a deliberate enactment of this House and not an oversight, when the Senate presumed to challenge that, even those of us who had been on the losing side of the vote in the House of Commons united to defeat the attempt of the Senate to change the will of this House as expressed by its elected representatives. I think all parties would agree this is not the kind of Senate we would like. We must approach any Senate reform with this in mind. Mr. Speaker, it is with some reluctance that I decided to take part in this debate because I for one think that the matter of the Senate has been settled once and for all, both by the report prepared by the joint committees on the constitution and by the many reports of constitutional conferences that took place at the end of the sixties.
That being said, I would not like either to go into historical considerations which prevailed in 1867 when that body called the Senate was created, at a time when Lower Canada was expressing very strong reservations about the fact that there was only one elected House and that the rights of Lower Canada and those of the Maritime provinces could suffer from that. It was then asked for the creation of a body whose members would be designated by the government, one that would represent the regions and ensure the protection of the rights of the minority.
I will not enter into the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) regarding the internal operations of the Senate and the many amendments pertaining to its operations or even its
Senate Reform
reform which have been presented by the constitutional affairs committee and which were also suggested in the course of certain debates in the Senate by the senators themselves, as they are very concerned with the welfare of their House. For example, on March 13, 1973, there was a debate there during which Senator Croll to whom reference was made previously, made very valuable comments on the future of the Senate such as he viewed it.
Therefore I will not enter into those arguments, since the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville gave us many details and many patterns according to which the Senate might evolve. Instead I shall lay the emphasis on the present operations of the Senate such as they affect us as members of this House.
The fact is that for many years, I can even say over the last fifty years, the Senate has been the target of many criticisms and rightly so. The then prime ministers had the unfortunate habit of systematically appointing to the Senate members of the party in power, which resulted in reducing the degree of competency to a lower level, when those members of Parliament or organizers were appointed only for the political favours they provided. But we must pay tribute to the last three or four prime ministers, particularly to the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who brought some changes in the way of viewing the Senate and the appointments to the Senate.
Indeed, they chose a new procedure, namely appointing resource persons, people from the community. The best example I have in mind is the appointment of the current Speaker of the Senate, the hon. Renaude Lapointe. Those are people who left their marks and who were working in the world of business. Some of them were working for the protection of the consumers, others for the press, as in the case of Mrs. Lapointe, others were involved in mining or in the legal sector, and many other fields of endeavour.
And that way, I believe, we now have a Senate with a degree of competence that all Canadians should be proud of. The Senate is now a resource organization that can be relied upon because it is composed of people with a very high degree of competence, and I can say that when I have problems dealing, for instance, with the Canadian constitution, I readily request the advice of the Senator Golden-berg or Senator Forsey who are people with a really penetrating knowledge of the constitution, or of labour relations in the case of Senator Goldenberg.

Order, please. I am prepared in these circumstances to listen to the point of order, but I think something should be made clear. The Standing Orders of the House provide a procedure whereby estimates are studied in the committee, amendments moved, and so forth, and if effective the estimates would be reported back to the House with amendments and then would have to be reinstated. I do not challenge the interest of the hon. member in raising this point of order; however the process has gone on for some time now. Undoubtedly there can be suggestions to improve the procedure, but it is a procedure that has been used several times in the past as a result of points of order.
The supply bill will be introduced today instead of tomorrow at the hour at which it is expected to be voted on. Furthermore, the supply bill will be debated in all stages tomorrow. This is moving further and further in the direction of getting away from the procedure we followed in the past. However, I wanted to be clear that at this moment the Standing Order is specific, that the duty of the Chair is to intervene and to put without debate or amendment all questions necessary to decide on the supplementary estimates that are before us.
The hon. member seeks the floor on a point of order. I have given three hon. members the floor on a point or order. Let us be clear that we should not be debating what we are doing, but continuing to speak about order, and if we are talking about improvements in the procedure for supply, these are procedures that have been not only in use for some time but in effect, in respect of these supplementary estimates which have been before standing committees, hon. members from all parties have been present there, have discussed them, have moved amendments to them, and so on, and at this point the final step is being taken.
The hon. member's point is well noted and continues to form part of the study which is going on to try to improve these procedures, but again I say that we cannot solve the problem entirely at this moment.

Authority to borrow sufficient new money to cover estimated financial requirements, together with a margin for contingencies, is normally sought and granted in one of the first appropriation acts of any fiscal year.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join with other members in commending the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) on bringing the question of the adoption across Canada of a universal telephone number before the House. The value of such a number is obvious. In an emergency people sometimes have difficulty finding the proper number to call. The idea of a central switchboard that would direct calls to the police, firefighting services, drug intervention centres, and poison control centres is a very good one.
Any legislation that we would pass would primarily apply to Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia in view of the jurisdiction we have over the principal telephone systems in those three provinces. Naturally legislation would have to be passed relating to other provinces that have their own telephone systems. I understand that most telephone companies in Canada are co-operating completely in establishing such a system. For example, Bell has new equipment in place to accommodate this single number emergency call.
There is one area in my riding where I hope within the next 12 months new equipment will be put in place to handle not only emergency calls but regular telephone calls. I refer to the Silver Water exchange at the west end of Manitoulin Island where, when equipment is out of service, a person has to drive 25 or 30 miles to re-establish contact, let alone call someone such as a doctor in cases of emergency. I am glad to know that Bell Canada is co-operating, and I hope they will continue to co-operate to the extent of establishing good, workable equipment in all areas, but especially in those rural areas of Canada that still lack proper telephone service.
I understand there is a problem with the bill as presently framed in that it should be an amendment to the Railway Act rather than the National Transportation Act. At the hon. member's suggestion perhaps the subject matter of the bill could be sent to committee rather than the bill itself, if it be the case that the provisions of the National Transportation Act are inappropriate.
To make adoption of this number successful the co-operation of the municipalities and regional governments would be required. It is not merely a case of passing federal legislation approving adoption of this number; there would have to be co-operation with the various municipal agencies such as fire departments, police, drug and poison control centres, and so on. However, any leadership that we would give at the federal level would surely only expedite matters.
I understand that the city of Vancouver has already ordered equipment to handle this universal emergency number, and installation of such equipment is also under consideration in the Cranbrook area. In Alberta, Calgary, Edmonton and Red Deer already have this kind of service under consideration. There are no cities in Saskatchewan that have this service available, but the Saskatchewan telephone system is prepared to offer the service if the

municipalities will make a commitment. Negotiations were under way to serve Regina and Saskatoon in 1973.
The hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore mentioned that in Winnipeg and Brandon this emergency service is available. In the province of Ontario it has been available in London and Kitchener, covering the services of the fire department, police, poison control centre, ambulance dispatch and so on. So some progress is being made, and any leadership given at the federal level would only speed the process across the country. It would also clear away any additional legislative red tape that might be holding things up. I conclude with those few comments. Mr. Speaker, I think this might help clear up the situation. The question arises concerning the point I raised about the power of the Minister of Finance to enter into an agreement to disperse funds paid into the consolidated revenue fund. However, I want to point out that the agreement
March 29, 1976

with the province of Ontario signed by the Minister of Finance was tabled only in mid-January after the bill had been passed. Parliament had no opportunity to determine what kind of model agreement could be entered into by the minister. There is nothing in Bill C-73 which applies to the share of any revenue.
Now I come back. Does parliament at this stage have the opportunity to authorize the minister to enter into such an agreement providing for the payment out? There is no doubt the minister is empowered under the bill to enter into an agreement with a province with regard to the anti-inflation measure, but the minister has no power whatsoever to pay out moneys under any formula, to any province, out of the consolidated revenue fund.
If that power is to exist, it must come by way of a recommendation from His Excellency. That was not provided for in the recommendation to Bill C-73. I do not care whether the minister claims he has power under Bill C-73. There is nothing in the recommendations concerning payment of the funds to a province.

There is, under section 4 of the Anti-Inflation Act, the power to enter into agreements. I refer to page 6 of Bill C-73, particularly to section 4(3). May I say I am not relying upon the first minor amendment that appears in the present bill. However, let us look at clause 6 of this particular bill which amends section 20 of the Anti-Inflation Act. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there we are right into the heart of the matter. Section 20(4) of Bill C-73, the Anti-Inflation Act, provides:
Where a person has contravened the guidelines by paying or crediting as compensation in the course of a business or as a dividend, an amount that exceeds the amount that he was, under the guidelines authorized to so pay or credit, the administrator may, if he is not satisfied that there are circumstances that, based on the particular facts of the situation, justify the person in so contravening the guidelines, make such order as he deems appropriate to accomplish either or both of the following objectives:
Then paragraph (b) states:
-where no order has been made by him pursuant to subsection (5) arising out of the same circumstances, to require the person to pay to Her Majesty in right of Canada or to withhold out of subsequent payments or credits of a like nature and pay to Her Majesty in right of Canada, an amount stated in the order equal to the whole or any portion of the excess payment or credit as estimated by the administrator.
That is the amount required to be paid to the government of Canada under the order of the administrator. Then there is the model agreement signed by the minister with the province which takes the amount paid under the order of the administrator and divides it with the province on some formula. This formula, this amendment in Bill C-89 is directly connected with that matter. As a matter of fact, section 20(4) (b) is repealed, and in addition sections 20(5) (b), 29(6) and 20(7) are repealed and replaced by sections of clause 6 in Bill C-89. It is precisely under these subparagraphs that the administrator's orders are made.
I ask: How can there be any greater and more direct connection between the two bills? Therefore, it is at this point there should be in the amending bill a provision that any moneys paid to the account of Her Majesty pursuant to
Anti-Inflation Act
such an order may be divided between the government of Canada and a province according to whatever agreements exists. For that there would have to be a recommendation from His Excellency. I think I have established the argument to make the connection between Bill C-89 and Bill C-73.

There are better ways of getting to the core of the criminal problem than using a sledgehammer on the innocent, law-abiding gun owner of this country. Surely the hunters, target-shooters and gun collectors are not criminals, Mr. Speaker. If we dealt with our killers and criminals in a firm, harsh way, it would be the first positive step in stemming the tide of rising murder and violence. The legitimate gun owner, in this particular case, should not be made the scapegoat.

The government has utilized a kid-glove policy in dealing with the criminal element in this country, and it now attempts to take it out on the legitimate gun owner. It has responded to the emotions of hysteria in relation to some dramatic episodes that have taken place in the last year or so. Had these episodes not involved the use of guns, they may have involved the use of some other weapon such as a bomb. My view is that if a person is bound to kill or has an absolute desire to kill, he will kill in one way or another, whether it be with a gun, a bomb, a sledgehammer, a knife or the fist. I endorse that, as I endorse the idea of a uniform, countrywide mechanism for the training and testing of individuals in safe gun-handling practices. I repeat that what we need is stricter enforcement of existing laws, and less coddling of criminals. Stricter gun laws will not cut crime, but proper enforcement of existing laws will.
Let me deal now for a few minutes with the legislation as it relates to civil rights. We have had a form of press censorship, which was debated in the House in the last month or so.
