April 1, 1976

sort, whether or not they technically amount to a question of privilege, pending such a decision it has always been the practice of the House, certainly whenever possible, to give an opportunity to the hon. members involved to expose their thinking and to make whatever explanations may be warranted in the circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, my comments will be brief. The purpose of this intervention, which has already been outlined to the Electoral Boundaries Commission on maps, is not to take issue with the proposed revisions of population distribution between the ridings of London East and London West. Rather it is to propose a simpler and less disruptive boundary between these two ridings while maintaining the same population distribution as proposed by the federal boundaries commission. It seems to me that one of the criteria which common sense would dictate should play a part in the considerations of the commissioners is that of minimizing the disruption of existing ridings.

After the election of 1968, the first in the newly created ridings of London East and London West which resulted from redistribution, considerable confusion existed in the minds of residents as to which riding they lived in, and this was evidenced by the substantial amount of misdirected mail and telephone calls which both members received. This has now diminished to the point where, eight years later, it is safe to say that 95 per cent of the constituents know in which constituency they live. While accepting that some disruption is necessary with redistribution, it is suggested that new boundaries should keep disruption to the absolute minimum.
The proposal I am advancing has absolutely no bearing on any boundary of these ridings except the joint boundary, the common north-south boundary, between London East and London West. In the commissioners' proposal, in the northern section of the riding they carved out a much larger chunk of London West than was necessary. Then in order to compensate for this excessive carving in the northern portion of the riding, they had to carve an equally large chunk out of London East in the Southern section.
I believe that the boundary which would be achieved by a much smaller adjustment in the northern section of the riding would be considerably fairer and more reasonable from the point of view of the residents of both these ridings. It is a simpler boundary since it follows well-known thoroughfares, makes use of well-known streets, and will be much clearer for the residents to understand than will watercourses, less well-known streets, or relatively unknown railroad tracks.
Now I make a political comment, Mr. Speaker. Both ridings were won by the same party in the last election by substantial margins, and I think the fact that both sitting members support the proposed revision that I am advancing is a clear indication that it is felt that there is virtually no political advantage to be gained from either set of redistributed boundaries.
We believe, and I propose to the House, that one of the criteria that should be urged upon the commissioners is the minimizing of disruption for existing constituents. It seems to me that the disruption should be minimized to the greatest extent possible, consistent with the achieving of a proper distribution balance between the existing ridings.
I would therefore urge upon the commissioners of the federal boundaries commission that they re-examine their proposed boundary between the ridings of London East and London West and alter it so as to minimize the disruption they are imposing upon the residents of both ridings, and achieve their desired population distribution by substantially moving back the boundary in the northerly section of the riding, keeping the existing boundary between the two ridings in the southerly portion of the riding.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I fully agree with the position you have taken. There is one point I want to make. There has been an attempt by hon. members of the opposition who have spoken on this question of privilege to suggest that parliamentary secretaries in some way are conspiring to defeat the role of the opposition. Surely, in committees, as in the House of Commons, we are involved in an adversary contest. The government attempts to pass its estimates or its legislation, and the opposition resists or opposes.
Apparently the opposition is not satisfied with the effectiveness of its role in opposition. It is the right of hon. members to be dissatisfied with that role, but surely it is the right of government supporters, backbenchers or parliamentary secretaries, to debate or ask questions in the committees in the same way as members of the opposition. Their behaviour in that regard should not in any way be taken as a conspiracy to defeat the opposition. That is the whole purpose of this House and its committees, namely, to present legislation on the part of the government and to oppose it on the part of the opposition.
Parliamentary secretaries, as well as backbenchers, have an obligation to support the government in measures presented to this House or to committees. It should not be suggested that because they participate in that role they are frustrating the opposition in its attempt to oppose the government.

To put the matter in perspective, it might be more appropriate to say that I have certain powers to permit or prohibit something here, but I do not have the same powers to permit or prohibit certain things in the standing committees.
The hon. member for St. John's East raised what the hon. member for Edmonton West described as a question of privilege. I should like to draw his attention to the fact that it was raised not as a question of privilege but as a point of order. I think that is quite proper. It concerns business in the standing committees. It relates to proceedings and in fact is a procedural question pure and simple. It is, in fact, a point of order concerning the privileges of hon. members. As others have said, if it is not a point of order, they would quite readily volunteer to put forward the matter as a question of privilege if that would change its character. I do not think it would.
Hon. members have said that when a parliamentary secretary asks questions of his own minister in a standing committee, in fact he interferes with their right as opposition members to ask questions. You do not have to go very far from that proposition to see the difficulty that precisely the same thing would apply if it were another government member proceeding to take up some of the time of the committee and asking the very same questions of the minister. I do not say that in an effort to put forward an argument on one side or the other of the case; I say it only to illustrate the impossible position in which hon. members are seeking to put the Chair by asking the Chair to pass judgment on a description, on a second-hand basis, of events which have taken place in the standing committee, a description-which is certainly far from agreed upon-of the argument and nature of the proceedings.
For many years in this House, the Chair has refrained from sitting in appeal on procedural decisions taken in standing committees. Hon. members are seeking my guidance as to what steps I would take if I were chairman of the standing committee involved. Surely hon. members have the intelligence to appreciate the reasoning, that I have exposed under considerable fire, in respect of my attitude toward the role of parliamentary secretaries at


proceedings over which I preside. However, with all due respect to hon. members who participated in this debate, let me point out that that is the limit of my authority, and unless procedural changes are made that remains the limit and I do not propose to attempt to exercise a non-existent authority to decide appeals of standing committees in procedural matters.
As I said, my reasoning is obvious and clear in respect of a situation in which one hon. member asks questions on one day and answers them on another. I exposed my reasoning on that, and one can only speculate as to what I would do if I were sitting in the chair of the standing committee involved. I do not propose to cross that line unless in some way members of the House deem it proper, in their wisdom, to amend the procedures that have been followed so carefully which keep the Chair out of questions of order-and essentially this is a very serious and important question of order-in the standing committees. A question of order it is, and the Chair will not sit in appeal on questions of order in standing committees.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I can see that it hurts them because they are always great ones to repeat this garbage, which in itself has nothing to do with Bill C-83.
The hon. member read the document into the record and I thought we should remind him that it is indeed capitalism that has been responsible for all these kinds of ills which he has read out as being so called revolutionary.
The government has presented Bill C-83 for parliament's consideration and decision. This piece of legislation comes under the general heading of peace and security. When we start thinking about peace and security we tend to think of widening police authority, prohibiting certain acts or instruments, and toughening penalties.
Our children and, I suppose, we as adults get a lot of romantic ideas from American television programs such as police shows, where in every case we see the police making an arrest we see them warning the arrested person of his right to remain silent and if he should say anything it could be used later on in prosecuting him. We do not have that right in Canada. As a matter of fact I know that our police force has indeed very wide powers, much wider than in the country to the south of us. So if we get a romantic view from television and think that Canadians also have these rights which we see on U.S. television, then we should be informed that such is not the case.
Not so long ago I had occasion to write to the Attorney General of the province of Ontario about the case of a young man who was arrested in a hotel in Sudbury and taken to the local jail. What was his offence? He was suspected of smoking grass in the hotel. He demanded to make one phone call to his lawyer, which he thought he had the right to do, but the police promptly booted him to the jail and told him he had no such right and he would stay in jail until they should decide what they would do with him.
The widening of police powers is one of the things that concerns many people in this country. In the bill before us the government seems intent on impressing on the Canadian people that it is the last buffer of security against a rising tide of crime and violence. Therein lies my first criticism of Bill C-83. It includes six particular items, from entirely new legislation governing the ownership of long guns, to amending present legislation covering habitual offenders and dangerous sexual offenders, electronic surveillance, special crime inquiries and custody and release of inmates.
April 12, 1976

Of all the items in Bill C-83 gun control has attracted by far the greatest attention, and in some parts of the country more than others. In my riding of Nickel Belt, which is predominantly rural and working class, there is great concern about certain provisions, which concern has resulted in about 180 pieces of mail daily, plus a 6,000 signature petition. I understand the basic resentment of the people in my area against certain provisions of the bill. They see it basically as legislation aimed at large urban centres like Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa, where a firearm is not looked on in the same manner as in rural areas. Indeed many of the folk in my area say that this legislation is for those urban crazies who do not know about or have any respect for firearms and who want to shoot each other. They feel they are being put through this bureaucracy for the sake of protecting urban dwellers from each other.
In Nickel Belt most of the workers are employed in mines or smelters, and when work is finished, or on week ends, hunting and fishing are indispensable forms of relaxation. Many of the workers have hunt camps or cottages and spend time in the summer and fall hunting and fishing.
They are also concerned about the cost of any kind of licensing program. One constituent pointed out to me that he now pays $15 for a moose licence, $5 for a licence for hunting migratory birds, and $10 for a deer licence, and after those costs there is also the cost of a hunting licence. Now there is a proposed gun licence fee which is as yet undetermined. My constituents see this additional cost a further proof that eventually hunting will be reserved for the rich.
My constituents have also expressed concern about the engulfing red tape of bureaucracy. By nature, rural folk seem to be much more resentful about encroaching bureaucracy than urban folk, probably because they are much more self reliant. In particular, they are set against the proposal to have two guarantors testifying as to the character of a prospective gun owner.
Concern has been expressed about the provision of search and seizure without warrant. In particular, if no charge has been laid, the firearm owner ought to be able to claim his property unless the licensing action is in progress or some charge has been laid.
Another question raised by my constituents deals with reimbursement. If, during the initial three year licensing period, a person is not issued a licence to own a firearm and the registrar issues an order to take his property, will that person be reimbursed? That is very important to the people in my constituency. I have met with members of rod and gun clubs and other interested citizens and listened to their opinions, and expressed mine, in the hope that this legislation can be as effective as possible.
I support the principle of gun control. Indeed the bill does not go far enough with respect to tightening gun control. I have said this to rod and gun clubs and those interested in my constituency, and there are large numbers of them.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, in considering the statement the minister has just made, the only thing I can say is that it is not worse than we anticipated, but obviously it does not make the situation much better. If the farmers of Canada supplying the dairy manufactur-
12776

April 13, 1976
Dairy Policy
ing industry were to receive $11.45 on 100 per cent of supply management quotas, those farmers would be very happy. The farmers do not receive that kind of money. While it is true that as a result of the government's policies we have been able to raise the price of industrial milk by 43 cents a hundred, we have at the same time reduced the anticipated size of global consumption as a result of increasing the price of butter by five cents and the price of skim milk powder by four cents. One of the problems results from the fact that the federal dairy policy does not, through market sharing quota arrangements, allow for a longer period of time, which is absolutely necessary in designing a program to meet the needs of dairy farmers.
The minister says we can increase production per cow. A dairy farmer operates on the basis of a herd and he has to make plans before deciding how much production he should have. If this is to be changed every three months, as has been the case in the past year, there is no way the dairy farmer can remain in a healthy state. For those farmers who are producing over 94.5 per cent of their quotas there will be a reduction, bringing the return below the farm cost of production. It would be much more honest on the part of the minister if rather than saying that the federal subsidy rate will be $2.66 per hundred, he had said the subsidy would be $1.31 on quota milk. Right now there is a deduction from all in-quota milk of $1.35, which leaves the federal subsidy at $1.31, not $2.66.
If we reduced the over-quota milk and the in-quota milk, the farmer would be left with something like 20 cents a hundred for producing milk. We should be very interested in this aspect of the matter because of its great implications not only for the dairy industry but in respect of the production of beef, pork and probably poultry as well.
If the farmer is to receive something in the neighbourhood of 20 cents a hundred for the milk he ships over quota, has $8.60 plus $1.31 deducted, and has to pay a transportation cost, he will find that shipping the milk to market will cost him money. The farmer is smart enough to know that he should buy a couple of pig's or start raising some veal. In this way the farmer will have to operate the dairy production safety valve on his own.
One of our major tasks in this country is to create a dairy industry that is able to meet Canadian requirements as well as producing for the export market. If a farmer has to decide, on a daily basis, how much milk he puts into the bulk tank, and knows if he puts too much in and only receives 20 cents per hundred it will cost him money, he will then open the safety valve and move into other production. This is particularly true if the farmer has to pay a transportation charge of, say, 75 cents. He will then end up with a net loss of considerably more than 50 cents. This will result in an increased production of beef, pork and poultry products.
As the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) said earlier, dairy farmers are concerned about the deal the minister made last November in relation to the export market. I gather from the November statement that we agreed to relate 10 per cent of our total manufactured dairy production to our imports of dairy products. The $50 million we have agreed to import in cheese production represents about 5 per cent of our manufactured production. It is not difficult to envisage that we will be importing other com-

modities, bringing us to that 10 per cent range without any exports at all.
Like the egg business, we have more exports than imports. We import eggs at the full table price but we export them at the breaker trade price. We export more eggs. But this is much like the skim milk powder business; we export a considerable amount of powder, but we do so at a loss. Who accepts that loss? I suggest it is not the government, but the loss is being absorbed by the farmers themselves.
I think it behooves every member of this House, whether interested in consumers or producers, to demand of the government that we develop a much more far-seeing dairy program than this, get away from the yearly quota and make a decision concerning what we anticipate to be the needs of the Canadian public. We should meet those needs and get whatever export sales we can. This should be done in conjunction with the provinces. The province of Ontario recently signed an agreement with the minister and that province is very unhappy with the agreement: it has written a long letter to the minister outlining ten or 12 reasons why it is dissatisfied. The province of Quebec has given the year's notice that will allow it to get out of the national share quota arrangement.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset permit me to establish my position. I will be opposing Bill C-311 because I do not feel we should have to pay people to become Canadian citizens. Certainly it would almost appear to be a shame for me this afternoon to have to oppose a private member's bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a gentleman whom I respect greatly as a member of this House. Ever since I came here as a new member I have had great admiration and respect for the proposer of Bill C-311. However, as I shall demonstrate in my remarks I do not feel this to be a wise move or one in which the government should be involved. It would place an additional burden on the employer by requesting that he expend additional funds to allow persons desirous of becoming Canadian citizens time off from their duties.
During the vote this afternoon I had time to reflect on the fact that since it is so rarely that the New Democratic Party votes against our government, it is almost a shame that I have to speak against Bill C-311 as proposed by the

hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, a member of that party.
However, one does wonder from time to time, when this type of suggestion is made in the House, whether it might just be another thread of the socialist fabric that we sometimes see appearing on the scene in Canada. Let me say, on behalf of the Liberal Party, that the buck stops here and we do not endorse or support this type of program. On the contrary, I would say we should be emphasizing and encouraging the necessity for greater productivity in this country. We have acknowledged and accepted our responsibility in this regard in this time of restraint. The restraint legislation, by the way, as stated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other authorities throughout the country is working, contrary to some of the mutterings by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and members on the other side of the House. However, it is always somewhat amusing to me to hear recommendations from the opposition parties for the spending of more money, or the spending of someone else's money, to be more precise.
Bill C-311 asks for a contribution of money to persons who aspire to be Canadians. That money will, of course, be spent by someone other than the New Democratic Party. It will be spent by employers and by people who will have to carry the burden.
Hon. members who have travelled throughout the world know only too well the feeling of pride one has on returning to one's native land. We acknowledge that pride when we think of the freedom, the good life, the prosperity, the availability of medicine and education, and all the excellent facilities and programs which are available to Canadians. I am hard put to understand why we should entertain Bill C-311 under which we would be reimbursing prospective Canadians.
I suppose it could be said, after listening to some of the allegations and innuendos from the other side of the House, that this could almost be considered a form of a bribe to entice an individual to become a Canadian. Perhaps that is an exaggeration, but there are some who have this type of warped mentality, and sometimes we witness it in the House.
However, if we consider this proposition, we would not want to support Bill C-311 because we would be encouraging a situation where we might be accused of offering some sort of incentive, which I suggest might be called a bribe, for someone to take on the great honour of becoming a Canadian citizen.
If we are going to encourage law, order, peace, security, and justice in Canada, as is the case we hope with the New Democratic Party, I think we should be urging programs which will encourage people to respect authority, to respect police, and to respect teachers in schools. That is the type of program we should be supporting, and we should not start new Canadians who are coming into the country and who want to become Canadians off on the wrong foot by giving them the impression that this is the way it works in Canada. They should not be given the impression that they can be paid to become Canadian citizens.

Order, please. Yesterday the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar raised a point of order at the conclusion of the question period in which he was supported by
Ministerial Responsibility
the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. Arguments were advanced in favour of a contrary opinion, and I undertook yesterday to give the matter careful review. That review included a reference to remarks I made in the House on April 14, 1975, which, as hon. members may recall, was just after the Easter recess of that year.
I made those remarks for two reasons. First, it was just at the time we had begun to operate under new procedures with respect to the question period and, second, as a new Speaker I felt hon. members would wish to know as soon as possible my attitude toward the handling of the question period. I attempted to make that statement a thorough review of my attitude toward questions that ought to be permitted. I tried to make it as positive as possible and in line with a theme different from that of the past. Instead of there being a number of restrictions such as had grown up, somewhat vaguely, affecting the right of members to put questions, I attempted to put forward a positive statement as to what could be done, rather than a negative statement expressing what could not be done.
In respect of the responsibility of ministers and the areas which could be covered, I said this as recorded at the top of page 4763 of Hansard of April 14, 1975:
Sixth, a question must be within the administrative responsibility of the government or the minister. Obviously, the government in general cannot be responsible for those areas which are beyond its own administrative responsibility. Furthermore, the minister to whom the question is directed is responsible to the House for his ministry; that is, his present ministry. He is responsible to the limits of that ministry, but not beyond that. In this regard I find no reason to change the earlier decision I made in respect of the capacities which ministers enjoyed in previously-held portfolios.
I think that statement is clear, and by and large it has not been challenged, I have to be concerned whether that ruling unduly restricts the right of members to put questions in respect of a situation facing us where information is sought about influence which members-indeed, ministers-might have exercised with respect to decisions affecting tenders. I am satisfied that the ruling I have quoted is a fair one still because, of course, questions can always be put to the Prime Minister concerning the conduct of any minister; questions can be put to the minister responsible for the tendering in the particular department involved, they can be put to the President of the Treasury Board with respect to general tendering practices, and they can certainly be put to the Solicitor General or to the Minister of Justice if there seems to be any suspicion of irregularity.
In some cases there is no doubt that questions are deflected to ministers who have served in previous capacities, but it seems to me that this is within the limits of jurisdictional responsibility as we have always known it and extends ample opportunity for hon. members to put questions at least during the question period. We have to remember, after all, that we are not attempting to afford complete investigative powers in the question period, but simply trying to manage the question period which is an extremely important aspect of our procedure and one whose duration each day is limited.
Finally, I am sure hon. members will understand that there are circumstances in which the enforcement of this rule is not easy for the Chair: ministers, in making one answer, may voluntarily go across the line and it is dif-

April 27, 1976
Energy Policy
ficult for the Chair to interrupt further questioning on the same point. There are also circumstances in which statements may be made by ministers with respect to their former capacities, and the Chair has to hear at least one or two preliminary questions in clarification of such statements before it can rule definitively that the questions appear to go beyond the limits of the administrative responsibility of the minister concerned. These do not constitute exceptions; they are simply circumstances which cause the Chair some difficulty in specific enforcement.
All members will, I hope, agree with the practice I have followed. When in doubt as to the acceptability of a question, I have sought to resolve that doubt in favour of the member putting the question, rather than the member having to answer it.

April 28, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
province of Ontario, in the cases of all of whom the opportunity to catch up in terms of salary and inflation had not been present in the way it was for the private sector.
Prior to October 14, two-thirds of the Ontario teachers had signed collective agreements which were predominantly in the 25 per cent to 30 per cent range for the first year of the contract. To restrict the other one-third to increases of 10 per cent to 12 per cent would have seriously impaired historical relationships by opening a 10 per cent to 20 per cent salary gap between teachers who had previously received similar salaries. If the article had been written with some honesty, I think the writer should have taken into account the fact that for historical reasons the school teachers in Ontario had not been able to catch up with the rest of the community but were in the course of doing so in this particular year. It was for that reason that the school teacher settlements have distorted the over-all settlements scrutinized by the Anti-Inflation Board.
By way of comparison, in the same period 18 non-teacher public sector cases covering only 1,776 employees came before the board. On average the award was 13.1 per cent, a rollback of 1.7 percentage points from demands of 14.8 per cent. This contrasts with total non-teacher awards of 14.6 per cent which were 1.9 percentage points below demands of 16.5 per cent. In other words, taking out the Ontario school teachers' case, because that particular group had not had an opportunity to catch up as had most others in the community, one can see that there was not in any sense an unbalanced favouring of the public sector over the private sector.
I am sure this article will continue to be quoted by hon. members. I think they should bear in mind, however, that the writer of the article, whether deliberately or otherwise, failed to take account of the distortion that was introduced because of the high school teachers' situation. If hon. members opposite want to say that the Toronto high school teachers, or Renfrew high school teachers and others in Ontario should not be permitted to catch up, that in those particular communities where, because of the accident of time they have not had the opportunity to catch up, that is one thing. If they agree, however, that this particular group had fallen behind and that some of their colleagues throughout the province had other chances to catch up and they were caught by the program in the middle, then I do not think they can fairly argue against the historical relationship exception being applied in their favour.

April 30, 1976
Medical Care Act
The present Medical Care Act calls for the federal government to pay 50 per cent of the costs of medical care which the provinces have to meet. Once this bill is in, there will be two choices. One of those choices hangs on the use of the phrase "the lesser of", so that in the end there is only one choice. The government will pay the lesser of two amounts, either 50 per cent of the total costs of the provinces or only so many more dollars than the provinces got last year. Even when the minister can stand up and talk about hundreds of millions of dollars more, the fact is that that sum of money will be less than would have been the case if this bill had not been brought in. We contend that this is a betrayal of the provinces and of the people of Canada. It is a going back on the principles which were established in the Medical Care Act after all the years it took us to get that legislation.
I join again with the hon. member for Athabasca in registering our protest against this legislation having been put through at the second reading stage by closure, and I join once again in saying that part of the trouble about this whole exercise is that it is a case of how not to conduct federal-provincial relations. The health ministers of the provinces have been most unhappy with the way they have been treated, especially since the announcement by Mr. Turner in the budget he brought down last June. We think the whole story is a sorry mess.
However, we have just about reached the end of the report stage of this bill, leaving the third reading stage to come later, possibly next Wednesday, although I understand that it may be shifted to Thursday, and in this final part of the debate on the report stage I think not only should I direct myself to the amendment proposed by the minister, but that I might once again summarize the choices which are before us right now. We have a government bill which proposes certain fixed percentages so far as the increases which can take place this year and next year are concerned. Then in that bill there is a provision that after that the government has the right, by order in council, to fix the ceilings. They can be anything. There could be consultation, but in the end the government makes the decision. That is the picture. This is a bill that in the first and second years has a precise limit, but in years three, four, five, six, seven and on is subject only to the dictatorial, unilateral decision of the government, which puts it into effect by order in council. That is the bill. I tried, by way of amendment, to kill the bill completely and leave the Medical Care Act as it stands. The voice vote was against my motion, and I suppose that may be the result when the recorded vote is taken.
The next position was that proposed by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), that reluctantly we accept years one and two with ceilings, but that the rest of the bill be cancelled; that there be no Bill C-68 after two years have gone by. That is not as desirable as my position,

namely, that the ceilings should be cancelled altogether, but it is a compromise that we can accept if we must. Again, the voice vote was against the motion and the government has shown no willingness to go the other way.
We come to two more propositions. One was the proposal in the motion of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Friesen) that a government order in council fixing the ceilings in years three, four, five, six, seven, and so on, not come into effect until parliament has voted on it. Yesterday the majority said no to that as well. We now have the proposal of the minister that the government shall have the right to bring in its orders in council in years three, four, five, six, seven, and so on, and put those into effect right away, subject only to the right of 50 members of the House of Commons to sign a motion which would result in a debate. If that debate were to go against the order in council, then it would have to be cancelled. I make the point, Mr. Speaker, that there is a tremendous difference between having the right to vote on the validity of those orders in council before they are put into effect and simply being given the right to do that after the horse has been stolen, as I said last night.
I think the least acceptable of the propositions is the one before us in the name of the minister. So long as the government that brought in the order in council has a majority in the House, it of course can expect to get its order in council approved. Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the motion on which I agree in principle. However, in view of the present economic conditions. I think it is impossible for the Farm Credit Corporation to increase its funds at the same pace as it thought it would. Actually, the corporation will not have enough funds to approve the same amount of credit as for 1975-76. In addition, since it had to carry certain amounts involved last year over its budget for this year, it is evident that the number of new loans should be reduced likewise.
I think that we should also urge farmers to take part in the anti-inflation program, much as we ask all groups in our society and all our industrial sectors to do. However I think that with all the new guidelines concerning farm credit it will be possible for us, while beating inflation, to reach certain goals.
Those aims have, I believe, been clearly defined in the criteria outlined by the Department of Agriculture. I am quoting only a few instances of the consolidation of applicants' debts. Formerly, it was possible for a farmer to gather all his debts and apply for a single loan which would take care of all the total indebtedness. Now we shall urge instead other loan companies to lend the money so that the corporation may pursue its activities and its aim of improving the agricultural production in this country. This is why we must earmark funds for those farmers who do not derive an adequate income from their operation and who wish to buy more land.
We shall not lend money so readily to those farmers who have enough land, assets and an adequate income.
Those who do not have enough land to farm are unable to derive an adequate income from farming will be particularly encouraged.
Moreover, we will give assistance to the younger people-and I often hear this comment in my constituency- because a young farmer today does not have enough money to buy land which costs more and more. Thus, we will grant loans particularly to one, two or three members of the same family who want to buy the family farm.
Mr. Speaker, I think that even though fewer will be available for farm credit, it will still be possible to help the farmers who either wish to improve their lot or simply to take up farming. In my opinion, this is one aspect of the problem facing the young farmers and those who are developing their operation.
We should not be concerned only with financing problems facing farmers but I believe that with provincial and perhaps even municipal authorities we should hold a joint meeting of the three levels of government with a view to constituting agricultural land banks.
In an area such as mine, even if farm credit is available to the farmers, it has become unthinkable to buy land
Farm Credit Act
because most if not all of it has passed into the hands of speculators. Even if he has already settled, a farmer cannot think of increasing his land, let alone a young man who intends to enter this industry. Therefore I believe the major problem does not exist at the credit level only but also extends to the possiblity of acquiring land.
Mr. Speaker, if we do not stop this shameful speculation which is now raging in the Montreal area, we will lose all the best agricultural land in Quebec.
I do not think we should dwell merely on the financial problem. We should rather consider the possibility now given to present and future farmers to buy new lands. And I would urge the committee on agriculture to look into this matter so as to be in a position to make recommendations to the provincial agriculture ministers and also to the municipal affairs ministers who are the only ones qualified and empowered to act in zoning matters.
Mr. Speaker, I think that if we could do as some American states have done and urge the provincial legislatures to intervene as some American states and zone certain agricultural areas, land speculation would no longer be possible in those regions.
So long as we do not come to grips with the financial problem, to earmark additional funds for the Farm Credit Corporation will only amount to overbidding.
I also think that we, as a government, should urge the lending institutions such as banks and trust companies to make more and more loans to the farmers who have always found it difficult to borrow money, and that is why they have always relied on the government. If we believe in our farming industry, I wonder why financial institutions such as banks are not more interested in this field, which proves most profitable. Unfortunately, one only has to consider the farming production surpluses last year.
Mr. Speaker, even if it is hard to tell the farmers that we cannot make more funds available to them, increase their borrowing power next year, I think they must agree to join us and the other sectors of the Canadian economy in our fight against inflation, a fight which has made a very good start with the results we already know, which gives us some hope of a decreasing rate of inflation this year.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the motion of my colleague, but with the present inflationary crisis, I have to say that however valuable this project may be, we will have to postpone it before adopting it.

The man who piloted this whole idea was Sir Adam Beck who, when he set up Ontario Hydro which has produced one of the greatest power systems on this continent, did it with the slogan "The gifts of nature belong to the people". That is still true. Whether it is coal, gas, oil, hydro or nuclear power, these belong to the people. This government and the provincial governments have a responsibility to see that the gifts of the people are developed for the benefit of the people.

Speech:
At last, Mr. Speaker, at long last someone else besides the federal government has recognized that there is an energy crisis in this country. The day of cheap energy is gone. The House, indeed the whole country, owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). However, it is unfortunate that his flash of brilliance did not continue into the second half of his motion where he failed to present some solution to the problem.
The motion under debate, Mr. Speaker, represents another attempt by the opposition to have the federal government come to the rescue because a provincial government has been unable to manage its own affairs. They would have us believe that the skyrocketing price of energy has come as a complete surprise, when in fact the handwriting has been on the wall for at least the last two and a half years.
As has already been pointed out, the responsibility for electrical power generation rests with the provincial governments. It was the provincial governments which decided to burn oil to produce electricity. Security of supply was of less importance than low price in the decision to rely on foreign imports rather than western Canadian crude oil.
While the dramatic price increases which resulted from the actions of the OPEC members could not have been foreseen, the possibility of such action taking place always existed and therefore should have been allowed for. The Atlantic provinces are now paying the price for having chosen the wrong long term option. If the hon. members opposite choose to see a statement of fact as representing a callous attitude, then they are unduly sensitive. The free enterprise system, which they admonish us not to destroy, rewards those who make the right decision and penalizes those who are wrong. Surely no one who loses money in the stock market expects to be bailed out.
The federal government is being asked to bail out the Atlantic provinces now that they are faced with a serious situation. The opposition fails to recognize, however, the fact that the federal government has initiated, during the

last two decades, a number of endeavours designed to provide that region with a stable and affordable source of electrical energy.
These have included loans under the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act totalling $225 million, grants of over $3 million to study the possibilities of tidal power, a loan of $350 million for the Point Lepreau nuclear plant, a grant toward the New Brunswick-Nova Scotia interconnection of $4 million, and a loan and grant totalling $27 million toward the P.E.I. interconnection with New Brunswick. As well, the federal government has contributed $120 million in oil import compensation for the production of electricity. Over-all financial assistance totals more than $1.2 billion.
In a further attempt to stabilize the price of electricity the federal government has pressed the maritime provinces since 1972 to co-operate in an inter-provincial grid and has offered funds to support the establishment of such a network. Another product of federal initiative, Petro-Canada, plans to devote $25 million or 25 per cent of its exploration budget over the next five years to exploration for oil and gas on the east coast. Until the discovery and development of significant reserves, though, the maritime provinces, and especially Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, will have to rely on existing energy sources. It will be several years before any alternative sources become available.
Considering Nova Scotia's abundant coal supply it would appear logical to devote a larger amount of that fuel to electricity production in order to decrease reliance on oil. However, this does not provide a short term solution. Problems are encountered in transportation, including the need for sea rather than rail transport, and the upgrading of port facilities. The process of converting generating plants from oil to coal burning would be expensive both in time and money. Problems of air pollution from the high sulphur content coal must also be considered. It may be reasonably assumed that a three to five year lead time would be required before the use of coal would alleviate the problems currently being experienced. I want to say for the benefit of the parliamentary secretary who is assigned to answer me that both I and Mr. Arvaluk are well aware of the process of receiving permits for exploration work in the North. What is at issue here is the government's discourtesy in not forewarning the ITC that these permits were coming forward, and the inexcusable action of the minister in not even being aware that they had been issued.
Also for the benefit of the parliamentary secretary I should like to give some background of this incident. It began several years ago when the department authorized a sum of money to be given to the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada for research into the land claims of the Inuit. After four years of work the ITC presented to cabinet its proposal for the settlement of Inuit land claims in the Northwest Territories. From the remarks made at that meeting on February 28 of this year I, and other observers, thought both sides were willing to co-operate with each other and that the negotiations for the Inuit land claim were off to an amiable start.
The government received the ITC proposal and said it would study it. The government even asked for some meetings to clarify parts of the proposal. I understand that one of those meetings has already taken place. As I said, this tells me that the negotiations over the Inuit land claims have started. On March 29, a series of exploration permits were issued. These were permits to explore for uranium, and they are by no means singular. The government has been issuing these things wholesale for the past several years-permits to drill for oil and gas in the Beaufort Sea, permission to carry out seismic testing in Lancaster Sound, and so on. However, there is a difference now. All that land is the subject of land claims negotiations.
I and the ITC, as well as many others, view the act of granting permits of this kind without informing the ITC as nothing but an act of extreme bad faith.
On April 6 the ITC delivered a letter to the minister to outline their grievance which, I repeat, is serious. It is felt that the whole negotiation is in jeopardy. The next day when I asked my question in the House the minister was not even aware of the matter. There is no excuse for this. The land claims issue should be of utmost importance to this department. The people concerned seem to be too busy handing out exploration permits to care about this matter.

Speech:
We do not
believe that aspects of life as important as physical fitness, amateur sport and recreation should be financed by gambling, which calls on the poor to pay for it, instead of taxation which is levied according to ability to pay.
We also feel therefore that this proposal to put the federal government into the lottery business for all time is economic retrogression of the worst kind. What is the point of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) announcing a budget in which he is going to propose tax measures, if the government is going to accept the proposition that when money is needed it can be raised through lotteries and gambling? It is a move completely in the wrong direction, and so far as the aspects of this proposal that relate to the future are concerned, we are opposed to them. This makes it clear that the government does not take physical fitness, amateur sport and recreation seriously, and it makes it clear that if the government gets into trouble with something else-health costs, veterans' pensions, or what have you-which it cannot afford, it will say, "We can go in for gambling again," and the whole business of taxation and redistribution of wealth in this country would be completely shot.
We find ourselves more or less in the position which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) indicated, namely, that this House may have to do something about the Olympic Games and should do something about the Commonwealth Games. But bring that proposition before us in clear terms, and do not ask us at the same time to commit Canada to a government lottery under federal authority on a permanent basis. We are completely opposed to such a regressive step.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to make a long speech at this time. Briefly, I want to make two points in answer to some of the contentions made by other hon. members of this House and raised in the debate. While I have served in two previous parliaments, this will be the first time I shall be called on to vote on this question.
Every elected member of a legislature, Mr. Speaker, has to answer to his or her conscience on the basic question of whether to lead or reflect public opinion. Many hon. members who have spoken in this debate-as nearly as I can tell, every one of them an abolitionist-cited Edmund Burke of a century and a half ago to the effect that it would be a matter of an individual member's conscience how he or she voted on an issue after being elected. With all due respect, I cannot accept this position in regard to capital punishment.
Over a number of years I have serious reservations about the effect of capital punishment and have never been persuaded that it is an effective deterrent. The long, statistical arguments, many of which have been reproduced, including some raised by the minister in introducing this debate, have to me been inconclusive. It seems to me that the increase or decrease of crime and violence is more related to fundamental social and economic conditions in the community than it is to absence or presence of capital punishment.
I do believe, however, that an elected representative must lead on occasion and also reflect public opinion on other occasions. Since the days of Edmund Burke, many things have changed. The electorate is much more literate, for better or for worse. Many more people follow public events and are better informed. Public opinion is now capable of being analysed and measured through the device of polling techniques. To say that the job of an elected representative is to pay no attention to public opinion, but simply to act according to his or her conscience will not, in my opinion, be good enough in this situation.
To me, sir, it is a basic principle that laws must be enacted with the consent of the governed. A law that is not

I can remember, also, the extent to which the law was violated, and the countless times reputable citizens in the community indicated their complete disrespect and contempt for the law. Eventually, despite the very convincing arguments of the dedicated people who were committed to the abolition of the use of alcohol, the law had to be changed. The law had to reflect the customs, attitudes and mores of the people to whom it applied.
The hon. gentleman who preceded me as the representative for Ottawa West conducted a poll and received the same kind of result that I did when I conducted a poll on this subject. In short, about 73 per cent of the 15 per cent of all households which responded in Ottawa West to a questionnaire distributed on postmen's walks were in favour of capital punishment for some situations involving, particularly, brutal and callous murder. The hon. gentleman who preceded me in office, when he faced this kind of result, said he did not care what the public thought and he would vote according to his conscience. I criticized him and said he could not, and should not, do that. I accept the consequences of the criticism I directed against him at that time when I now face, in this House, the responsibility of voting. All the evidence which I have seen from Gallup polls or any other source indicates that the majority of people in our society favour capital punishment being limited to extreme cases.
There are those who say contemptuously that an elected representative is not a mere opinion poll-taker, not a mere automatic reflection of measured public opinion. This goes without saying; there is no argument about it. But it is a long way to go from that position to the extreme argument that public opinion itself can be disregarded.
I have consulted my voters on a few basic issues of conscience-on gun control, on abortion and on capital punishment. I do not propose to consult them on day-today items of legislation because it is practically impossible to do so. It seems to me, however, that the consultation process should be applied on basic moral questions in the community, and legislators have to give careful attention to the results of this consultation process.

Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I think that the distinction between class one and class two murder is a desirable feature of the bill. I do not believe, however, that it serves the interests of rehabilitation or of developing within prison institutions the atmosphere in which rehabilitation of other prisoners is possible if we stick to these long, minimum terms. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think that the 25-year sentence was designed to make abolition palatable and acceptable to the community. BasePK: 3033000

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have this opportunity to say a few words in this debate on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I will read the motion so that it will form part of the speech I will send to my constituents in order that they will know what remarks I have made in this House. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should immediately introduce legislation to implement the resolutions of the Yukon Territorial Council and the Northwest Territorial Council requesting that the government apply those principles of constitutional and democratic development that will establish a fully representative and responsible system of government to the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories respectively.
This is a very important motion and I am happy to see it debated here. It is time that something was done to change the situation in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. We have a colonial situation. Although we have fully elected bodies, they can be overruled by an appointed civil servant. That is an intolerable situation in this day and age.
I believe, as I am sure many other northerners believe, that we can capably look after our own affairs in both territories. Many people doubt whether we can pay our own way. If we are not doing so now, we certainly could with the utilization of the natural resources in that part of the country.
We are only asking for a democratic right that most Canadians now enjoy. What kind of government would be most suitable is a point that could be debated. Certainly it should be one that is fully responsible, with full taxation powers and so on. The argument about there not being a big enough population does not hold water.
I remind the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) of a certain visit to the north. I was happy to hear him refer to a visit to the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I remind him of what took place at Whitehorse in the Yukon on December 12, 1972. At that time the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development was travelling in the north. The hon. member will recall a motion passed by that committee, which was chaired by the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan). I am sure the hon. member for Gaspe voted in favour of that resolution calling for full responsible government for the Yukon. The hon. member now seems to speak completely against what he voted for in the Yukon. He said one thing when he was in the north, and now says something else when he is here.
